title: Define an algorithm. Write any four characteristics of a good algorithm.
chunks: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure or set of rules to be followed in calculations or other problem-solving operations. Characteristics: Finiteness: Must terminate after a finite number of steps. Definiteness: Each step must be precisely defined. Input: Has zero or more inputs. Output: Produces one or more outputs. Effectiveness: Operations must be basic enough to be done exactly and in finite time.
subject: daa

title: What is pseudocode? Mention two advantages of representing an algorithm using pseudocode.
chunks: Pseudocode is an informal, high-level description of the operating principle of a computer program or algorithm. Advantages: Easier for humans to read and understand compared to actual code. Independent of any specific programming language, making it versatile.
subject: daa

title: Differentiate between time complexity and space complexity with one example.
chunks: Time Complexity: The amount of time an algorithm takes to run as a function of the length of the input. Space Complexity: The amount of memory an algorithm requires to run as a function of the length of the input. Example: Mergesort has a time complexity of O(n log n) and space complexity of O(n), whereas Bubble sort has time complexity O(n^2) but space complexity O(1).
subject: daa

title: Define Big-O notation.
chunks: Big-O notation is a mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular value or infinity. In computer science, it is used to classify algorithms according to how their run time or space requirements grow as the input size grows. It describes the upper bound of the complexity.
subject: daa

title: What is the difference between best-case, worst-case, and average-case analysis?
chunks: Best-case: The minimum time required for program execution for any input of size n. Worst-case: The maximum time required for program execution for any input of size n. (Provides an upper bound). Average-case: The expected time required for program execution over all possible inputs of size n.
subject: daa

title: What is asymptotic analysis? Why is it preferred over measuring execution time?
chunks: Asymptotic analysis evaluates the performance of an algorithm in terms of input size (n) as it approaches infinity. It is preferred because execution time depends on hardware, compiler, and OS, whereas asymptotic analysis provides a machine-independent way to compare algorithms' efficiency.
subject: daa

title: What is amortized analysis? Explain the aggregate method in one or two sentences.
chunks: Amortized analysis calculates the average time taken per operation, over a sequence of operations, guaranteeing the average performance even if a single operation is expensive. Aggregate method: It computes the total time T(n) for a sequence of n operations and sets the amortized cost per operation to T(n)/n .

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= n; j++) { count++; } }
chunks: The outer loop runs n times. For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs n times. Total iterations = n * n = n 2 . Final time complexity: O(n 2 ) .

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= i; j++) { count++; } }

title: Define algorithm correctness. Differentiate between partial correctness and total correctness with suitable examples.
chunks: Algorithm Correctness: An algorithm is correct if, for every valid input, it halts and produces the correct output as defined by its specifications. Partial Correctness: If the algorithm halts, it produces the correct output (but it might not halt). Example: A while(true) loop that searches for an element and breaks when found. If the element isn't there, it might loop forever. Total Correctness: The algorithm is guaranteed to halt, and when it halts, it produces the correct output. Example: A standard for-loop based linear search that scans an array from start to end and returns true/false.
subject: daa

title: What is a loop invariant? Explain the three steps—initialization, maintenance, and termination—used to prove the correctness of an algorithm.
chunks: A loop invariant is a condition or property that is true before and after each iteration of a loop. It is used to prove the correctness of loop structures. Initialization: The invariant must be true before the first iteration of the loop. Maintenance: If it is true before an iteration of the loop, it remains true before the next iteration. Termination: When the loop terminates, the invariant gives us a useful property that helps show the algorithm is correct.
subject: daa

title: Explain how loop invariants can be used to prove the correctness of a sorting algorithm.
chunks: In sorting algorithms like Insertion Sort, a loop invariant can be defined as: 'At the start of each iteration i , the subarray A[0...i-1] consists of the elements originally in A[0...i-1], but in sorted order.' Initialization: For i=1, A[0] is just a single element, which is trivially sorted. Maintenance: During iteration i , the algorithm inserts A[i] into its correct position in A[0...i-1], making A[0...i] sorted. Termination: The loop ends when i = n. The invariant states that A[0...n-1] is sorted, which means the entire array is sorted, proving correctness.

title: Define the Divide and Conquer paradigm. Explain its three basic steps with a suitable example.
chunks: Divide and Conquer Paradigm The Divide and Conquer paradigm is an algorithmic design strategy that solves a problem by recursively breaking it down into two or more sub-problems of the same or related type, until these become simple enough to be solved directly. The solutions to the sub-problems are then combined to give a solution to the original problem. It consists of three basic steps: Divide: Break the given problem into smaller sub-problems. Conquer: Recursively solve these sub-problems. If the sub-problem size is small enough, solve it directly (base case). Combine: Merge the solutions of the sub-problems to form the solution of the original problem. Example: Merge Sort In Merge Sort: Divide: Divide the unsorted array of size n into two sub-arrays of size n/2 . Conquer: Recursively sort the two sub-arrays using Merge Sort. Combine: Merge the two sorted sub-arrays into a single sorted array.
subject: daa

title: What are the divide, conquer, and combine steps in a Divide and Conquer algorithm?
chunks: The three main steps of the Divide and Conquer strategy are: Divide: This step involves breaking the original problem into a set of smaller sub-problems. The sub-problems should represent a smaller instance of the same original problem. Conquer: This step involves solving the sub-problems recursively. If the sub-problem is small enough (the base case), it is solved directly without further division. Combine: This step involves taking the solutions to the sub-problems and merging them together to formulate the solution to the original problem.
subject: daa

title: Explain the general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm. How is it different from an iterative algorithm?
chunks: General Structure The general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm can be represented recursively: Algorithm DAndC(P) { if Small(P) then return S(P); // Solve directly else { Divide P into smaller instances P1, P2, ..., Pk, k ≥ 1; Apply DAndC to each of these subproblems; return Combine(DAndC(P1), DAndC(P2), ..., DAndC(Pk)); } } Difference from Iterative Algorithms Control Flow: Divide and Conquer algorithms rely heavily on recursion (functions calling themselves), whereas iterative algorithms use loops (for, while) to repeat tasks. State Management: In recursion, state is maintained implicitly by the call stack. In iteration, variables explicitly hold state (like loop counters). Approach: Divide and conquer works top-down (breaking large to small), while dynamic programming or iterative methods can work bottom-up (solving small to build large).
subject: daa

title: Identify whether the following algorithms use the Divide and Conquer technique. Give reasons for your answer: Binary Search, Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Bubble Sort
chunks: Binary Search: Yes . It divides the array into two halves, compares the target with the middle element, and recursively conquers only one of the halves. The combine step is trivial (returning the index). Merge Sort: Yes . It divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts each half (conquer), and then merges the two sorted halves (combine). Quick Sort: Yes . It chooses a pivot to divide the array into two partitions (smaller than pivot and greater than pivot), recursively sorts the partitions (conquer). Combine is trivial as sorting is done in place. Bubble Sort: No . It is an iterative comparison-based algorithm that repeatedly swaps adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order. It does not divide the problem into smaller subproblems or use recursion.
subject: daa

title: Explain the advantages and limitations of the Divide and Conquer approach.
chunks: Advantages Solving Complex Problems: Makes solving conceptually difficult problems easier by breaking them down into simpler, smaller sub-problems. Parallelism: Sub-problems are independent and can often be executed in parallel on multi-core processors. Memory Access Efficiency: Can be designed to optimize cache usage, as smaller sub-problems fit easily into the CPU cache. Efficiency: Often yields algorithms with faster time complexities, e.g., reducing O(n²) to O(n log n) in sorting. Limitations Overhead: The recursion and function call stack overhead can make them slower for small inputs compared to simple iterative approaches. Space Complexity: Deep recursion trees can lead to stack overflow or require excessive auxiliary space. Repeated Subproblems: If not careful, overlapping subproblems can be solved multiple times, leading to inefficiencies (better handled by Dynamic Programming).
subject: daa

title: What is a recurrence relation? Explain its role in analyzing the time complexity of recursive algorithms.
chunks: A recurrence relation is an equation or inequality that describes a mathematical function in terms of its value on smaller inputs. Role in Analyzing Time Complexity: When an algorithm contains a recursive call, its running time can be described by a recurrence relation. For example, in Merge Sort, solving a problem of size n involves two subproblems of size n/2 , and merging takes linear time O(n) . This gives the recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) By solving this recurrence relation (using methods like the Substitution Method, Recursion Tree Method, or Master Theorem), we can express the time complexity of the algorithm in Big-O notation (e.g., O(n log n)).
subject: daa

title: Solve the following recurrence using the substitution method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
chunks: Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n Guess: T(n) = O(n log n). We need to prove that T(n) ≤ c · n log n for some constant c > 0. Proof by induction: Assume the bound holds for n/2, i.e., T(n/2) ≤ c · (n/2) log(n/2). Substitute this into the recurrence: T(n) ≤ 2 · [c · (n/2) log(n/2)] + n T(n) ≤ c · n log(n/2) + n T(n) ≤ c · n(log n - log 2) + n T(n) ≤ c · n log n - c · n + n We want T(n) ≤ c · n log n. This holds true if: c · n log n - c · n + n ≤ c · n log n -c · n + n ≤ 0 c ≥ 1 Since we can choose c ≥ 1, the guess is correct. Result: T(n) = O(n log n)
subject: daa

title: Solve the following recurrence using the substitution method: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1
chunks: Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 Guess: T(n) = O(log n). We prove T(n) ≤ c · log n for some constant c. Proof by induction: Assume T(n/2) ≤ c · log(n/2) Substitute into recurrence: T(n) ≤ c · log(n/2) + 1 T(n) ≤ c · (log n - 1) + 1 T(n) ≤ c · log n - c + 1 We want T(n) ≤ c · log n. This requires: - c + 1 ≤ 0 ⇒ c ≥ 1 Since we can find a constant c (c ≥ 1) such that the condition holds, the guess is correct. Result: T(n) = O(log n)
subject: daa

title: Solve the following recurrence using the Master Method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
chunks: The Master Theorem applies to recurrences of the form: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) Given: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n a = 2 b = 2 f(n) = n Calculate n log b a : n log 2 2 = n 1 = n Compare f(n) with n log b a : f(n) = n, and n log b a = n. They are equal, which matches Case 2 of the Master Theorem (f(n) = Θ(n log b a )). Formula for Case 2: T(n) = Θ(n log b a log n) Result: T(n) = Θ(n log n)
subject: daa

title: Solve the following recurrence using the Master Method: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n
chunks: Given: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n a = 4 b = 2 f(n) = n Calculate n log b a : n log 2 4 = n 2 Compare f(n) with n log b a : f(n) = O(n 2 - ε ) for ε = 1. Since f(n) grows polynomially slower than n log b a , this is Case 1 of the Master Theorem. Formula for Case 1: T(n) = Θ(n log b a ) Result: T(n) = Θ(n 2 )

title: Solve the following recurrence using the Master Method: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n²

title: Solve the following recurrence using the Master Method: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1
chunks: Given: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 a = 1 b = 2 f(n) = 1 (which is n 0 ) Calculate n log b a : n log 2 1 = n 0 = 1 Compare f(n) with n log b a : f(n) = 1, and n log b a = 1. title: Explain why Binary Search requires the input array to be sorted. What happens if Binary Search is applied to an unsorted array?
chunks: Why Sorting is Required: Binary search fundamentally relies on the ordering of elements. It compares the target value to the middle element and mathematically eliminates half of the remaining search space based on that comparison. If target < mid , it knows the target must be in the left half, because all elements in the left half are smaller than the middle element. If Applied to an Unsorted Array: The logic breaks down. Comparing the target to the middle element gives no reliable information about where the target might be located in the rest of the array. The search might discard the half that actually contains the target, leading to a false negative (returning "not found" even when the element exists).
subject: daa

title: Explain how the Divide and Conquer technique can be used to find the maximum and minimum elements of an array.
chunks: The Divide and Conquer Max-Min algorithm finds both the maximum and minimum elements simultaneously by recursively breaking the array into halves. Divide: Split the array into two halves. Conquer: Recursively find the (max, min) pair for the left half and the (max, min) pair for the right half. Base Cases: If the subarray has 1 element, return it as both max and min. If the subarray has 2 elements, compare them and return the larger as max and the smaller as min. Combine: Compare the max of the left half with the max of the right half to get the overall max. Compare the min of the left half with the min of the right half to get the overall min.
subject: daa

title: Explain the best-case, average-case, and worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort.
chunks: Best Case: O(n log n) Occurs when the pivot chosen at each step divides the array into two roughly equal halves. The recursion tree has a depth of log(n) and partitioning at each level takes O(n) time. Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) Average Case: O(n log n) Occurs when the pivot randomly divides the array into proportional splits (e.g., 9-to-1 split or 3-to-1 split). Even an unbalanced split like 99-to-1 results in an O(n log n) running time, as the depth of the tree is bounded by a logarithmic function. Worst Case: O(n²) Occurs when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element, leading to completely unbalanced partitions (one sub-array of size n-1, and one of size 0). This creates a skewed recursion tree of depth n. Example: sorting an already sorted array when the first or last element is chosen as the pivot. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n)

title: Compare conventional matrix multiplication and Strassen's Matrix Multiplication with respect to the number of multiplications and asymptotic time complexity.
chunks: Feature Conventional Matrix Multiplication Strassen's Matrix Multiplication Method Uses 3 nested loops to compute dot products of rows and columns. Uses Divide and Conquer, breaking n x n matrices into 4 (n/2 x n/2) sub-matrices. Multiplications per step 8 multiplications for a 2x2 division step. 7 multiplications for a 2x2 division step (optimized mathematically). Additions/Subtractions 4 additions. 18 additions/subtractions (increased overhead). Recurrence Relation T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²) T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²) Asymptotic Time Complexity O(n 3 ) O(n log 2 7 ) ≈ O(n 2.81 ) Conclusion: Strassen's algorithm reduces the number of recursive multiplications from 8 to 7, bringing down the asymptotic time complexity. However, due to the overhead of extra additions, it is practically faster only for very large matrices.

title: Explain how the Divide and Conquer technique can be used for multiplication of large integers.
chunks: When integers are very large (e.g., hundreds of digits in cryptography), standard multiplication (O(n²)) is too slow. The Divide and Conquer technique (Karatsuba algorithm) speeds this up. Process: Divide: Split each n-digit number into two halves (high and low parts). Example: X = A*10^(n/2) + B and Y = C*10^(n/2) + D Standard Divide and Conquer: Compute four partial products (AC, AD, BC, BD). This yields T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n²). Karatsuba Optimization: Compute only three products recursively: P1 = A * C P2 = B * D P3 = (A + B) * (C + D) The middle term (AD + BC) is derived as P3 - P1 - P2 . Conquer and Combine: This reduces the recurrence to T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) , improving the time complexity to O(n log 2 3 ) ≈ O(n 1.585 ).

title: Is merge sort a stable sorting algorithm? Explain.
chunks: Yes, Merge Sort is a stable sorting algorithm. Explanation: A sorting algorithm is stable if it preserves the relative order of equal elements. In Merge Sort, stability is maintained during the merge step. When combining two sorted sub-arrays, if elements are equal, the element from the left sub-array (which appeared earlier in the original array) is explicitly chosen to be placed into the merged array first. By doing this, the original relative ordering of equal elements is preserved.
subject: daa

title: When would you select merge sort instead of quick sort?
chunks: Merge Sort is preferred over Quick Sort in the following scenarios: Stability is Required: Merge Sort is inherently stable, whereas Quick Sort is not. Worst-Case Guarantees: Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in all cases. Quick Sort can degrade to O(n²) in the worst case (e.g., already sorted arrays with bad pivot choice). Sorting Linked Lists: Merge Sort performs excellently on linked lists because elements don't need contiguous memory access for random swaps (unlike Quick Sort). The O(n) auxiliary space requirement of Merge Sort is also reduced to O(1) for linked lists. External Sorting: When the dataset is too large to fit in RAM and resides on disk, Merge Sort's predictable sequential access patterns make it the preferred choice.

Unit I: Introduction & Sorting Algorithm An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure or set of rules to be followed in calculations or other problem-solving operations. Characteristics: Finiteness: Must terminate after a finite number of steps. Definiteness: Each step must be precisely defined. Input: Has zero or more inputs. Output: Produces one or more outputs. Effectiveness: Operations must be basic enough to be done exactly and in finite time. Pseudocode Pseudocode is an informal, high-level description of the operating principle of a computer program or algorithm. Advantages: Easier for humans to read and understand compared to actual code. Independent of any specific programming language, making it versatile. Time complexity and space complexity Time Complexity: The amount of time an algorithm takes to run as a function of the length of the input. Space Complexity: The amount of memory an algorithm requires to run as a function of the length of the input. Example: Mergesort has a time complexity of O(n log n) and space complexity of O(n), whereas Bubble sort has time complexity O(n^2) but space complexity O(1). Big-O notation Big-O notation is a mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular

value or infinity. In computer science, it is used to classify algorithms according to how their run time or space requirements grow as the input size grows. It describes the upper bound of the complexity. Best-case, worst-case, and average-case analysis Best-case: The minimum time required for program execution for any input of size n. Worst-case: The maximum time required for program execution for any input of size n. (Provides an upper bound). Average-case: The expected time required for program execution over all possible inputs of size n. Asymptotic analysis Asymptotic analysis evaluates the performance of an algorithm in terms of input size (n) as it approaches infinity. It is preferred because execution time depends on hardware, compiler, and OS, whereas asymptotic analysis provides a machine-independent way to compare algorithms' efficiency. Amortized analysis Amortized analysis calculates the average time taken per operation, over a sequence of operations, guaranteeing the average performance even if a single operation is expensive. Aggregate method: It computes the total time T(n) for a sequence of n operations and sets the amortized cost per operation to T(n)/n . Find the time complexity of the following code: sum = 0; a = 5; b = 10; sum =

a + b; printf("%d", sum); The time complexity is O(1) (constant time) because there are no loops or recursion. The number of basic operations (assignments, addition, printing) is fixed and independent of any input size. Find the time complexity of the following code: if (n > 100) x = x + 1; else x = x - 1; Also mention the best and worst case The time complexity is O(1) . The condition evaluation takes O(1) time, and both the if block and else block contain basic arithmetic operations taking O(1) time. Best case: O(1) Worst case: O(1) Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { printf("%d", i); } The loop variable i goes from 1 to n , incrementing by 1 each time. The loop runs exactly n times. Number of iterations: n . Final time complexity: O(n) . Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 2) { count++; } The loop variable i starts at 1 and increases by 2 in each iteration (1, 3, 5, ..., n). The loop runs roughly n/2 times. Execution count: n/2 times. Final time complexity: O(n) . Find the time complexity:

for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= n; j++) { count++; } } The outer loop runs n times. For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs n times. Total iterations = n * n = n 2 . Final time complexity: O(n 2 ) . Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= i; j++) { count++; } } The outer loop runs n times. The inner loop runs i times. The total number of executions is the sum of the first n integers: Summation: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 = (n 2 + n)/2 . Final time complexity: O(n 2 ) . Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i = i * 2) { printf("%d", i); } The loop variable i starts at 1 and multiplies by 2 each time. Sequence of i values: 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., 2 k . The loop terminates when 2 k > n, which means k ≈ log 2 (n). The total iterations is roughly log 2 (n). Final time complexity: O(log n)

Unit II: Divide & Conquer Algorithm correctness Algorithm Correctness: An algorithm is correct if, for every valid input, it halts and produces the correct output as defined by its specifications. Partial Correctness: If the algorithm halts, it produces the correct output (but it might not halt). Example: A while(true) loop that searches for an element and breaks when found. If the element isn't there, it might loop forever. Total Correctness: The algorithm is guaranteed to halt, and when it halts, it produces the correct output. Example: A standard for-loop based linear search that scans an array from start to end and returns true/false. Loop invariant A loop invariant is a condition or property that is true before and after each iteration of a loop. It is used to prove the correctness of loop structures. Initialization: The invariant must be true before the first iteration of the loop. Maintenance: If it is true before an iteration of the loop, it remains true before the next iteration. Termination: When the loop terminates, the invariant gives us a useful property that helps show the algorithm is correct. Loop invariants can be used to prove the correctness of a sorting algorithm In sorting algorithms

like Insertion Sort, a loop invariant can be defined as: 'At the start of each iteration i , the subarray A[0...i-1] consists of the elements originally in A[0...i-1], but in sorted order.' Initialization: For i=1, A[0] is just a single element, which is trivially sorted. Maintenance: During iteration i , the algorithm inserts A[i] into its correct position in A[0...i-1], making A[0...i] sorted. Termination: The loop ends when i = n. The invariant states that A[0...n-1] is sorted, which means the entire array is sorted, proving correctness. Unit III: Greedy & Dynamic Divide and Conquer paradigm

Divide and Conquer Paradigm The Divide and Conquer paradigm is an algorithmic design strategy that solves a problem by recursively breaking it down into two or more sub-problems of the same or related type, until these become simple enough to be solved directly. The solutions to the sub-problems are then combined to give a solution to the original problem. It consists of three basic steps: Divide: Break the given problem into smaller sub-problems. Conquer: Recursively solve these sub-problems. If the sub-problem size is small enough, solve it directly (base case). Combine: Merge the solutions of the sub-problems to form the solution of the original problem. Example: Merge Sort In Merge Sort: Divide: Divide the unsorted array of size n into two sub-arrays of size n/2 . Conquer: Recursively sort the two sub-arrays using Merge Sort. Combine: Merge the two sorted sub-arrays into a single sorted array. Divide, conquer, and combine steps in a Divide and Conquer algorithm The three main steps of the Divide and Conquer strategy are: Divide: This step involves breaking the original problem into a set of smaller sub-problems. The sub-problems should represent a smaller instance of the same original problem. Conquer: This step involves solving the sub-problems recursively. If the sub-problem is small enough (the base case), it is solved directly without further division. Combine: This step involves taking the solutions to the sub-problems and merging them together to formulate the solution to the original problem. General structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm

General Structure The general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm can be represented recursively: Algorithm DAndC(P) { if Small(P) then return S(P); // Solve directly else { Divide P into smaller instances P1, P2, ..., Pk, k ≥ 1; Apply DAndC to each of these subproblems; return Combine(DAndC(P1), DAndC(P2), ..., DAndC(Pk)); } } Difference from Iterative Algorithms Control Flow: Divide and Conquer algorithms rely heavily on recursion (functions calling themselves), whereas iterative algorithms use loops (for, while) to repeat tasks. State Management: In recursion, state is maintained implicitly by the call stack. In iteration, variables explicitly hold state (like loop counters). Approach: Divide and conquer works top-down (breaking large to small), while dynamic programming or iterative methods can work bottom-up (solving small to build large). Identify whether the following algorithms use the Divide and Conquer technique Binary Search: Yes . It divides the array into two halves, compares the target with the middle element, and recursively conquers only one of the halves. The combine step is trivial (returning the index). Merge Sort: Yes . It divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts each half (conquer), and then merges the two sorted halves (combine). Quick Sort: Yes . It

chooses a pivot to divide the array into two partitions (smaller than pivot and greater than pivot), recursively sorts the partitions (conquer). Combine is trivial as sorting is done in place. Bubble Sort: No . It is an iterative comparison-based algorithm that repeatedly swaps adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order. It does not divide the problem into smaller subproblems or use recursion. Advantages and limitations of the Divide and Conquer approach

Advantages Solving Complex Problems: Makes solving conceptually difficult problems easier by breaking them down into simpler, smaller sub-problems. Parallelism: Sub-problems are independent and can often be executed in parallel on multi-core processors. Memory Access Efficiency: Can be designed to optimize cache usage, as smaller sub-problems fit easily into the CPU cache. Efficiency: Often yields algorithms with faster time complexities, e.g., reducing O(n²) to O(n log n) in sorting. Limitations Overhead: The recursion and function call stack overhead can make them slower for small inputs compared to simple iterative approaches. Space Complexity: Deep recursion trees can lead to stack overflow or require excessive auxiliary space. Repeated Subproblems: If not careful, overlapping subproblems can be solved multiple times, leading to inefficiencies (better handled by Dynamic Programming). Recurrence relation A recurrence relation is an equation or inequality that describes a mathematical function in terms of its value on smaller inputs. Role in Analyzing Time Complexity: When an algorithm contains a recursive call, its running time can be described by a recurrence relation. For example, in Merge Sort, solving a problem of size n involves two subproblems of size n/2 , and merging takes linear time O(n) . This gives the recurrence: T(n) =

2T(n/2) + O(n) By solving this recurrence relation (using methods like the Substitution Method, Recursion Tree Method, or Master Theorem), we can express the time complexity of the algorithm in Big-O notation (e.g., O(n log n)). Solve the following recurrence Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n Guess: T(n) = O(n log n). We need to prove that T(n) ≤ c · n log n for some constant c > 0. Proof by induction: Assume the bound holds for n/2, i.e., T(n/2) ≤ c · (n/2) log(n/2). Substitute this into the recurrence: T(n) ≤ 2 · [c · (n/2) log(n/2)] + n T(n) ≤ c · n log(n/2) + n T(n) ≤ c · n(log n - log 2) + n T(n) ≤ c · n log n - c · n + n We want T(n) ≤ c · n log n. This holds true if: c · n log n - c · n + n ≤ c · n log n -c · n + n ≤ 0 c ≥ 1 Since we can choose c ≥ 1, the guess is correct. Result: T(n) = O(n log n) Solve the following recurrence Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1

Guess: T(n) = O(log n). We prove T(n) ≤ c · log n for some constant c. This requires: - c + 1 ≤ 0 ⇒ c ≥ 1 Since we can find a constant c (c ≥ 1) such that the condition holds, the guess is correct. They are equal, which matches Case 2 of the Master Theorem (f(n) = Θ(n log b a )). Formula for Case 2: T(n) = Θ(n log b a log n) Result: T(n) = Θ(n

They are equal, which matches Case 2 of the Master Theorem (f(n) = Θ(n log b a )). Linear Search and Binary Search Search Type Best-Case Average-Case Worst-Case Prerequisite Linear Search O(1) (Item is at index 0) O(n) (Item is in the middle) O(n) (Item is at the end or not present) None (Works on unsorted arrays) Binary Search O(1) (Item is the middle element) O(log n) O(log n) (Item is at extremes or not present) Array must be sorted Why Binary Search requires the input array to be sorted Why Sorting is Required: Binary search fundamentally relies on the ordering of elements. It compares the target value to the middle element and mathematically eliminates half of the remaining search space based on that comparison. If target < mid , it knows the target must be in the left half, because all elements in the left half are smaller than the middle element. If Applied to an Unsorted

Array: The logic breaks down. Comparing the target to the middle element gives no reliable information about where the target might be located in the rest of the array. The search might discard the half that actually contains the target, leading to a false negative (returning "not found" even when the element exists). Divide and Conquer technique can be used to find the maximum and minimum elements of an array The Divide and Conquer Max-Min algorithm finds both the maximum and minimum elements simultaneously by recursively breaking the array into halves. Divide: Split the array into two halves. Conquer: Recursively find the (max, min) pair for the left half and the (max, min) pair for the right half. Base Cases: If the subarray has 1 element, return it as both max and min. If the subarray has 2 elements, compare them and return the larger as max and the smaller as min. Combine: Compare the max of the left half with the max of the right half to get the overall max. Compare the min of the left half with the min of the right half to get the overall min. Combining all partitions Final sorted array: [5, 11, 12, 22, 25, 34, 43, 64, 78, 90] Best-case, average-case, and worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort

Best Case: O(n log n) Occurs when the pivot chosen at each step divides the array into two roughly equal halves. The recursion tree has a depth of log(n) and partitioning at each level takes O(n) time. Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) Average Case: O(n log n) Occurs when the pivot randomly divides the array into proportional splits (e.g., 9-to-1 split or 3-to-1 split). Even an unbalanced split like 99-to-1 results in an O(n log n) running time, as the depth of the tree is bounded by a logarithmic function. Worst Case: O(n²) Occurs when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element, leading to completely unbalanced partitions (one sub-array of size n-1, and one of size 0). This creates a skewed recursion tree of depth n. Example: sorting an already sorted array when the first or last element is chosen as the pivot. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) Conventional matrix multiplication and Strassen's Matrix Multiplication Feature Conventional Matrix Multiplication Strassen's Matrix Multiplication Method Uses 3 nested loops to compute dot products of rows and columns. Uses Divide and Conquer, breaking n x n matrices into 4 (n/2 x n/2) sub-matrices. Multiplications per step 8 multiplications for

a 2x2 division step. 7 multiplications for a 2x2 division step (optimized mathematically). Additions/Subtractions 4 additions. 18 additions/subtractions (increased overhead). Recurrence Relation T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²) T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²) Asymptotic Time Complexity O(n 3 ) O(n log 2 7 ) ≈ O(n 2.81 ) Conclusion: Strassen's algorithm reduces the number of recursive multiplications from 8 to 7, bringing down the asymptotic time complexity. However, due to the overhead of extra additions, it is practically faster only for very large matrices. Divide and Conquer technique can be used for multiplication of large integers When integers are very large (e.g., hundreds of digits in cryptography), standard multiplication (O(n²)) is too slow. The Divide and Conquer technique (Karatsuba algorithm) speeds this up. Process: Divide: Split each n-digit number into two halves (high and low parts). Example: X = A*10^(n/2) + B and Y = C*10^(n/2) + D Standard Divide and Conquer: Compute four partial products (AC, AD, BC, BD). This yields T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n²). Karatsuba Optimization: Compute only three products recursively: P1 = A * C P2 = B * D P3 = (A + B) * (C + D) The middle term (AD + BC)

is derived as P3 - P1 - P2 . Conquer and Combine: This reduces the recurrence to T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) , improving the time complexity to O(n log 2 3 ) ≈ O(n 1.585 ). Is merge sort a stable sorting algorithm Yes, Merge Sort is a stable sorting algorithm. Explanation: A sorting algorithm is stable if it preserves the relative order of equal elements. In Merge Sort, stability is maintained during the merge step. When combining two sorted sub-arrays, if elements are equal, the element from the left sub-array (which appeared earlier in the original array) is explicitly chosen to be placed into the merged array first. By doing this, the original relative ordering of equal elements is preserved. When would you select merge sort instead of quick sort Merge Sort is preferred over Quick Sort in the following scenarios: Stability is Required: Merge Sort is inherently stable, whereas Quick Sort is not. Worst-Case Guarantees: Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in all cases. Quick Sort can degrade to O(n²) in the worst case (e.g., already sorted arrays with bad pivot choice). Sorting Linked Lists: Merge Sort performs excellently on linked lists because elements don't

need contiguous memory access for random swaps (unlike Quick Sort). The O(n) auxiliary space requirement of Merge Sort is also reduced to O(1) for linked lists. External Sorting: When the dataset is too large to fit in RAM and resides on disk, Merge Sort's predictable sequential access patterns make it the preferred choice.

title: What is a DBMS? Discuss its advantages over a traditional file-processing system.
chunks: Definition A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that interacts with end-users, applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze data. It allows users to create, read, update, and delete data in a database. Advantages over File-Processing Data Redundancy and Inconsistency: Centralizes data, eliminating duplicate files and ensuring updates propagate everywhere. Data Isolation: Applications do not need to know the physical structure of the data files. Integrity Problems: Allows defining explicit integrity constraints (e.g., account balance > 0). Security Problems: Offers fine-grained access control and user authorization. Concurrent Access: Manages simultaneous access securely, preventing anomalies.
subject: dbms

title: What do you mean by data redundancy and data inconsistency? How does a DBMS take care of these problems?
chunks: Definitions Data Redundancy: The unnecessary duplication of data in a database. (e.g., storing a student's address in both the Library and Department files). Data Inconsistency: A consequence of redundancy where different copies of the same data hold different values (e.g., address updated in Library but not Department). DBMS Solution A DBMS minimizes redundancy by storing a single, centralized copy of the data (Data Normalization). Because there is only one authoritative copy, inconsistency is inherently prevented.
subject: dbms

title: Give the difference between a database system and a file-based system.
chunks: Differences Structure: DB systems store data in structured formats (tables/graphs); File systems store data in plain text/binary files. Data Independence: DB systems separate applications from data structure; File systems tightly couple applications to file formats. Querying: DB systems provide robust query languages (SQL); File systems require custom application code to extract data.
subject: dbms

title: Draw and explain the three-level (ANSI-SPARC) architecture of a DBMS.
chunks: The Three Levels External Level (View Level): The highest level, describing only the part of the database relevant to a specific user group (hiding the rest). Conceptual Level (Logical Level): Describes what data is stored in the entire database and the relationships among those data. Used by DBAs. Internal Level (Physical Level): Describes exactly how the data is physically stored on disk (data structures, file organizations). Exam Tip: The primary objective of this architecture is to achieve Data Independence .
subject: dbms

title: What is data abstraction? Discuss the three levels of data abstraction used in a DBMS.
chunks: Definition Data abstraction is the process of hiding complex internal data structures and storage details from the user, presenting only a simplified, usable view of the data. Three Levels Physical Level: Hides the complexity of block structures, indexing, and bytes on disk. Logical Level: Hides physical storage but reveals entities, data types, and relationships. Developers interact here. View Level: Hides the entire logical schema except for specific fields the end-user is authorized to see (e.g., a teller seeing only names and balances).
subject: dbms

title: Define the terms schema and instance. Why is this distinction important?
chunks: Definition Schema: The overall logical design/blueprint of the database. It changes rarely. Instance: The snapshot of data residing in the database at a specific moment in time. It changes frequently. Importance This distinction is crucial for maintaining data independence—altering the schema (like adding a column) should not arbitrarily destroy the existing instances.
subject: dbms

title: What is data independence? Explain logical and physical data independence with a suitable example.
chunks: Definition Data independence is the ability to modify a schema definition in one level without affecting a schema definition in the next higher level. Types Physical Data Independence: Ability to modify the internal/physical schema without altering the conceptual schema. Example: Changing a file from sequential to a B+ tree index to improve performance; application code doesn't change. Logical Data Independence: Ability to modify the conceptual schema without altering the external schema (user views). Example: Splitting an Employee table into two normalized tables; the original view can be maintained using a SQL JOIN, shielding the frontend application.
subject: dbms

title: Who are the different types of database users? Briefly describe the role of each.
chunks: Types of Users Parametric (Naive) Users: End-users who interact via standard GUI applications without knowing SQL (e.g., Bank Tellers). Application Programmers: Software engineers who write the backend logic connecting to the DB. Sophisticated Users: Analysts who interact directly with the DB using SQL queries to generate reports. Database Administrators (DBA): IT professionals who manage security, schemas, and performance tuning.
subject: dbms

title: List the responsibilities of a Database Administrator (DBA).
chunks: Responsibilities Schema definition and modification. Defining storage structures and access methods (indexing). Granting user authority and managing access security. Routine maintenance, database backups, and performance monitoring.
subject: dbms

title: Compare the hierarchical, network, relational and object-oriented data models. Which one is most widely used today and why?
chunks: Comparison Hierarchical: Data organized in a tree structure (1:N relationships). Fast but inflexible; requires navigating rigid pointers. Network: Data organized in a graph (M:N relationships allowed). Highly complex and difficult to maintain. Relational: Data organized in 2D tables (relations). Uses declarative SQL. Extremely flexible and mathematically sound. Object-Oriented: Data stored as objects with methods, matching OOP languages. Best for complex data (e.g., CAD/CAM). Most Widely Used The Relational Model is most widely used today due to its simplicity, robust theoretical foundation (normalization), and standard interface (SQL) which provides unparalleled data independence.
subject: dbms

title: State the advantages of the relational model over the other data models.
chunks: Advantages Simplicity: Uses a simple tabular structure (rows and columns) that is easy to understand compared to complex graph/tree pointers. Flexibility: Supports ad-hoc querying using standard SQL. Data Independence: Strong separation between logical representation and physical storage.
subject: dbms

title: Explain the terms super key, candidate key, primary key and foreign key with a suitable example.
chunks: Explanation Super Key: Any combination of columns that uniquely identifies a row. (e.g., StudentID + Name ) Candidate Key: A minimal super key; it uniquely identifies a row with no unnecessary columns. (e.g., StudentID or Email ) Primary Key: The specific candidate key chosen to identify rows. Cannot be NULL. (e.g., StudentID ) Foreign Key: A column that refers to the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity. (e.g., Dept_ID in a Student table referencing the Department table)
subject: dbms

title: What are integrity constraints in a relational model? Explain domain, key, entity and referential integrity.
chunks: Definition Integrity constraints are rules applied to a database to ensure the data is accurate, consistent, and valid. The Four Constraints Domain Constraint: Restricts the values a column can hold to a valid set (e.g., Age must be a positive integer). Key Constraint: Ensures that candidate/primary keys are completely unique for every row. Entity Integrity: States that no part of a Primary Key can be NULL, because a NULL value cannot uniquely identify a row. Referential Integrity: States that if a foreign key exists in a relation, its value must either match a primary key value in the referenced relation or be NULL. (e.g., You cannot enroll a student in a non-existent Course_ID).
subject: dbms

title: What is an E-R model? List the notations used to represent an E-R diagram.
chunks: Definition The Entity-Relationship (E-R) model is a high-level conceptual data model that visually represents entities (objects) and the relationships between them. Notations Rectangle: Entity sets Ellipse: Attributes Diamond: Relationship sets Lines: Link attributes to entities and entities to relationships
subject: dbms

title: Define entity, entity set, attribute and relationship, and illustrate each with a small diagram.
chunks: Definitions Entity: A real-world object with independent existence (e.g., a specific student). Entity Set: A collection of similar entities (e.g., all Students). Attribute: A property describing an entity (e.g., Name, Age). Relationship: An association among two or more entities (e.g., Student Enroll Course).
subject: dbms

title: Explain the different types of attributes, simple, composite, derived, multivalued and key attribute, with examples.
chunks: Attribute Types Simple: Indivisible atomic values (e.g., Gender ). Composite: Can be broken down into sub-parts (e.g., Name into First Name, Last Name). Derived: Calculated from other attributes; not physically stored (e.g., Age derived from DOB). Multivalued: Can hold multiple values for a single entity (e.g., Phone_Numbers ). Key: Uniquely identifies the entity (e.g., Roll_No ).
subject: dbms

title: What are the different types of relationships that can exist between two entities? Explain with diagrams.
chunks: Cardinality Ratios One-to-One (1:1): One entity in A is associated with at most one in B. (e.g., Department 1:1 Manager). One-to-Many (1:N): One entity in A is associated with many in B. (e.g., Department 1:N Employees). Many-to-Many (M:N): Many entities in A associated with many in B. (e.g., Student M:N Course).
subject: dbms

title: What is a weak entity set? Give a suitable example.
chunks: Definition A weak entity set lacks sufficient attributes to form a primary key. It depends on a strong entity (identifying owner) and uses the owner's key plus its own partial key to identify rows. Example A Dependent (spouse/child) of an Employee. The dependent is identified by combining their Name (partial key) with the owner's Employee ID.
subject: dbms

title: Explain unary, binary and ternary relationships with the help of diagrams.
chunks: Degrees of Relationships Unary (Degree 1): Relationship between instances of a single entity set (e.g., Employee Manages Employee). Binary (Degree 2): Relationship between two entity sets (e.g., Student Takes Course). Ternary (Degree 3): Relationship connecting three entity sets simultaneously (e.g., Supplier Supplies Part To Project). Exam Tip: A ternary relationship is not just three binary relationships; it represents a single fact involving all three entities together.
subject: dbms

title: Differentiate between total participation and partial participation constraints in an E-R diagram.
chunks: Differentiation Total Participation (Mandatory): Every entity MUST participate in at least one relationship. Indicated by a double line. (e.g., Every Employee must belong to a Department). Partial Participation (Optional): Only some entities may participate. Indicated by a single line. (e.g., Only some Employees are Managers of a Department).
subject: dbms

title: Explain generalization and specialization in the Extended E-R model with an example of each.
chunks: Specialization (Top-Down) The process of defining a set of subclasses from a single entity type (the superclass). It involves identifying characteristics that distinguish some entities in the set from others. Example: An Employee superclass can be specialized into Engineer , Manager , and Technician subclasses based on job role. Generalization (Bottom-Up) The reverse process of specialization. Multiple entity types with common attributes are synthesized into a single, generalized superclass. Example: Car and Truck entities share attributes like Vehicle_ID and Price, so they can be generalized into a Vehicle superclass.
subject: dbms

title: What is the difference between overlapping and disjoint specialization? Illustrate with an example.
chunks: Disjoint Specialization An entity can be a member of at most one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by a 'd' in the circle. Example: An Employee can be either an Hourly_Employee or a Salaried_Employee , but never both at the same time. Overlapping Specialization An entity may be a member of more than one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by an 'o' in the circle. Example: A Person can simultaneously be an Alumnus and an Employee of a university.
subject: dbms

title: What is aggregation in E-R modelling? When is it required? Explain with an example.
chunks: Definition Aggregation is an abstraction where a relationship set (and its associated entities) is treated as a higher-level entity set. When is it required? The basic E-R model cannot express relationships among relationships. Aggregation is required when a relationship between two entities needs to participate in another relationship with a third entity. Example Consider Employee working on a Project . This forms the relationship Works_On . If we want to record the Manager who oversees this specific (Employee-Project) assignment, we aggregate Works_On into a single entity, and create a new relationship Manages between it and Manager .
subject: dbms

title: Explain the concept of mapping cardinality with neat diagrams.
chunks: Definition Mapping cardinality (or cardinality ratio) expresses the number of entities to which another entity can be associated via a relationship set. Types One-to-One (1:1): An entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B, and vice versa. One-to-Many (1:N): An entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B. An entity in B is associated with at most one entity in A. Many-to-One (N:1): An entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B. An entity in B is associated with any number of entities in A. Many-to-Many (M:N): An entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B, and vice versa.
subject: dbms

title: What is a functional dependency? Why is it important in the process of database design?
chunks: Definition A functional dependency (FD) is a constraint between two sets of attributes in a relation. If A → B (A determines B), then for every valid instance of the relation, any two tuples that agree on the attribute A must also agree on the attribute B. Importance Functional dependencies are the theoretical bedrock of Normalization . They are used to specify constraints on data, discover candidate keys, and decompose relations to eliminate redundancy and update anomalies.
subject: dbms

title: What are insertion, deletion and update anomalies? How does normalization help remove them?
chunks: The Three Anomalies Update Anomaly: If data is stored redundantly, changing it in one row requires changing it in all rows. Missing one causes inconsistency (e.g., changing a department's location). Insertion Anomaly: The inability to add data to the database due to absence of other data (e.g., unable to add a new Department because it has no Employees yet, and Employee_ID is the primary key). Deletion Anomaly: The unintended loss of data when deleting a row (e.g., deleting the only employee in a department also deletes the department's information). How Normalization Helps Normalization resolves these by decomposing large, poorly structured tables into smaller, well-structured tables where each table represents a single logical theme or entity. By linking them with foreign keys, redundancy is eliminated, which inherently solves update, insertion, and deletion anomalies.
subject: dbms

title: What is normalization? Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF with a suitable example.
chunks: Definition Normalization is the process of organizing data to minimize redundancy and eliminate anomalies by dividing larger tables into smaller tables and defining relationships between them using functional dependencies. The Normal Forms First Normal Form (1NF): All attributes must be atomic (indivisible). No repeating groups or arrays allowed in a cell. Second Normal Form (2NF): Must be in 1NF, and all non-key attributes must be fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key. (Eliminates partial dependencies). Third Normal Form (3NF): Must be in 2NF, and no non-key attribute can be dependent on another non-key attribute. (Eliminates transitive dependencies: X → Y and Y → Z).
subject: dbms

title: Define BCNF. How is it different from 3NF? Support your answer with an example.
chunks: Definition Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X must be a super key. It is a stronger, stricter version of 3NF. Difference from 3NF 3NF allows a dependency X → Y where X is NOT a super key, provided that Y is a prime attribute (part of a candidate key). BCNF does not allow this exception. A table can be in 3NF but fail BCNF if it has overlapping candidate keys. Example Consider Relation(Student, Course, Instructor) . Keys are (Student, Course) and (Student, Instructor). FD: Instructor → Course . It is in 3NF because Course is a prime attribute. However, it violates BCNF because Instructor is not a super key.
subject: dbms

title: Write a short note on 4NF and 5NF, with an example of each.
chunks: Fourth Normal Form (4NF) Deals with Multi-valued Dependencies (MVD) . A table is in 4NF if it is in BCNF and contains no non-trivial multi-valued dependencies (where one attribute determines a set of values for another, independent of a third). Example: An Employee has multiple Skills and multiple Dependents. Storing them in one table creates massive redundancy. We split into (Emp, Skill) and (Emp, Dependent) . Fifth Normal Form (5NF) Deals with Join Dependencies . Also known as Project-Join Normal Form (PJNF). A table is in 5NF if it is in 4NF and cannot be decomposed into smaller tables without losing data (lossless join). It ensures that all join dependencies are implied by candidate keys.
subject: dbms

title: What is lossless-join decomposition? Explain with an example.
chunks: Definition Lossless-join decomposition means that if a relation R is decomposed into R1 and R2, joining them back together via a Natural Join will yield the exact original relation R, without any missing rows (loss of data) or extra spurious rows (creation of invalid data). Condition The decomposition is lossless if the common attribute(s) between R1 and R2 form a super key for either R1 or R2. (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 OR R1 ∩ R2 → R2). Example Splitting Employee(ID, Name, Dept, Dept_Location) into Emp(ID, Name, Dept) and Department(Dept, Dept_Location) is lossless because their intersection, Dept , is a primary key for the Department table.
subject: dbms

title: Define dependency-preserving decomposition and give a suitable example.
chunks: Definition A decomposition is dependency-preserving if the union of the functional dependencies in the decomposed relations logically implies all the functional dependencies of the original relation. This ensures that updates can be checked for validity without joining the tables back together. Example Original Relation: R(A, B, C) Functional Dependencies (FDs): A → B, B → C Decomposition: R1(A, B) and R2(B, C). FDs in R1: A → B. FDs in R2: B → C. Since (A → B) ∪ (B → C) covers all original FDs, it is a dependency-preserving decomposition .
subject: dbms

title: Consider an unnormalized relation Student_Marks(Rollno, Name, Subject, Marks) where a student appears in multiple rows, one per subject. Normalize it step by step up to 3NF, clearly stating the functional dependencies you have assumed.
chunks: Functional Dependencies (FDs) Assumed FDs based on logic: FD1: Rollno → Name (A student has one name) FD2: Rollno, Subject → Marks (A specific student's marks in a specific subject) The primary key for the unnormalized relation is (Rollno, Subject) . Step 1: 1NF to 2NF In the original relation, Name depends ONLY on Rollno , which is a part of the primary key. This is a Partial Dependency . We decompose to eliminate it: Student ( Rollno , Name) Performance ( Rollno, Subject , Marks) Step 2: 2NF to 3NF In the new tables, there are no non-key attributes depending on other non-key attributes (no transitive dependencies). Therefore, the tables are already in 3NF .
subject: dbms

title: A hostel management register stores the occupants of each room as shown in the table below. Redesign this data into a table that satisfies 1NF.
chunks: Problem Context In the unnormalized table, a single cell (like "Occupants") contains multiple values (e.g., "Alice, Bob"), which violates the atomicity rule of 1NF. 1NF Solution To convert to 1NF, we eliminate repeating groups by ensuring each cell holds only a single, atomic value. We duplicate the room number for each occupant. Room_No Occupant 101 Alice 101 Bob 102 Charlie Now, the primary key becomes the composite key (Room_No, Occupant) .
subject: dbms

title: The table below has the composite key (StudentID, SubjectID). Identify the partial dependencies present and decompose the table into 2NF.
chunks: Identifying Partial Dependencies Suppose the relation is R(StudentID, SubjectID, StudentName, Grade) . The primary key is (StudentID, SubjectID) . StudentID → StudentName (StudentName depends only on part of the key) — Partial Dependency StudentID, SubjectID → Grade (Grade depends on the whole key) — Full Dependency Decomposition into 2NF We split the table to remove the partial dependency: Student ( StudentID , StudentName) Enrollment ( StudentID, SubjectID , Grade) Both tables are now in 2NF as all non-prime attributes fully depend on their respective primary keys.
subject: dbms

title: The table below has EmployeeID as its primary key. Show that it violates 3NF, and decompose it into a set of tables that satisfy 3NF.
chunks: Violation of 3NF Consider Employee(EmpID, Name, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID is the primary key. Functional Dependencies: 1. EmpID → DeptID 2. DeptID → DeptName Because EmpID → DeptName through DeptID , this is a Transitive Dependency . 3NF forbids non-prime attributes depending on other non-prime attributes. Decomposition into 3NF We decompose the relation to separate the department details: Employee ( EmpID , Name, DeptID ) Department ( DeptID , DeptName)
subject: dbms

title: In the table below, each mentor teaches only one subject. Given that the candidate keys of this table are (StudentID, Subject) and (StudentID, Mentor), check whether it satisfies BCNF. If it does not, decompose it into BCNF.
chunks: Checking BCNF Relation: R(StudentID, Subject, Mentor) FDs: {StudentID, Subject} → Mentor , and Mentor → Subject (each mentor teaches one subject). Because Mentor → Subject exists, but Mentor is not a super key , the table violates BCNF (even though it is in 3NF since Subject is a prime attribute). BCNF Decomposition We must pull the violating determinant out into its own table: Mentor_Subject ( Mentor , Subject) Student_Mentor ( StudentID, Mentor ) Now all determinants are candidate keys.
subject: dbms

title: The table below stores a student's hobbies and the languages they know together, forcing every combination to be listed. Explain why this table is not in 4NF, and decompose it into a form that satisfies 4NF.
chunks: Violation of 4NF Relation: R(StudentID, Hobby, Language) A student's hobbies are completely independent of the languages they speak. This creates two Multi-Valued Dependencies (MVDs) : StudentID ⟶ Hobby and StudentID ⟶ Language . Storing them together forces a Cartesian product (e.g., 2 hobbies × 3 languages = 6 rows for one student). Since 4NF forbids non-trivial MVDs, this violates 4NF. 4NF Decomposition Split into two tables to eliminate the Cartesian product: Student_Hobby ( StudentID, Hobby ) Student_Language ( StudentID, Language )
subject: dbms

title: Given a relation R(A, B, C, D, E) with the functional dependency set F = {A -> B, BC -> D, D -> E}, compute the closure of {A, C} and state whether {A, C} is a candidate key of R.
chunks: Computing {A, C} + Start with the base set: {A, C} Using A → B , add B. The set becomes {A, B, C} Using BC → D (we have both B and C), add D. The set becomes {A, B, C, D} Using D → E , add E. The set becomes {A, B, C, D, E} Conclusion Since the closure of {A, C} contains all the attributes of the relation R, {A, C} is a super key . Assuming no proper subset of {A, C} can determine all attributes, {A, C} is a Candidate Key .
subject: dbms

title: Consider the relation Student_Course(Roll_No, Course_ID, Course_Name, Instructor) with the functional dependencies {Roll_No, Course_ID} -> Instructor, and Course_ID -> Course_Name. Identify the partial dependency present, show why the relation is not in 2NF, and decompose it into 2NF.
chunks: Analysis Primary Key: (Roll_No, Course_ID) The FD Course_ID → Course_Name is a Partial Dependency because Course_Name depends only on a part of the primary key (Course_ID), violating 2NF. 2NF Decomposition Course ( Course_ID , Course_Name) Student_Course ( Roll_No, Course_ID , Instructor) Now, both relations are in 2NF.
subject: dbms

title: Consider the relation Employee(Emp_ID, Emp_Name, Dept_ID, Dept_Name, Dept_Location) with the functional dependencies Emp_ID -> Emp_Name, Dept_ID and Dept_ID -> Dept_Name, Dept_Location. Show that this relation is in 2NF but violates 3NF, and decompose it into 3NF.
chunks: Analysis Primary Key: Emp_ID . Since the key is a single attribute, there are no partial dependencies, so it is in 2NF . However, the FD Dept_ID → Dept_Name, Dept_Location creates a Transitive Dependency (Emp_ID → Dept_ID → Dept_Name). This violates 3NF. 3NF Decomposition Employee ( Emp_ID , Emp_Name, Dept_ID ) Department ( Dept_ID , Dept_Name, Dept_Location)
subject: dbms

title: Consider the relation R(Student, Subject, Teacher) with the functional dependencies {Student, Subject} -> Teacher and Teacher -> Subject. Determine whether R is in BCNF. If it is not, decompose it into a set of relations that are in BCNF.
chunks: Analysis Candidate Keys: (Student, Subject) and (Student, Teacher) . For the FD Teacher → Subject , Teacher is a determinant but not a super key . Therefore, R violates BCNF. BCNF Decomposition Teach_Subj ( Teacher , Subject) Stud_Teach ( Student, Teacher ) Both tables are now strictly in BCNF.
subject: dbms

title: Given a relation R(A, B, C, D) with the functional dependency set F = {AB -> C, C -> D, D -> A}, find all the candidate keys of R and state the highest normal form it satisfies.
chunks: Candidate Keys {A, B} + = {A, B, C, D} {B, C} + = {A, B, C, D} (since C → D and D → A) {B, D} + = {A, B, C, D} (since D → A and AB → C) The candidate keys are AB, BC, and BD . All attributes are prime attributes except none (every attribute is part of at least one candidate key). Highest Normal Form Because there are no non-prime attributes, the relation is automatically in 3NF . However, check BCNF: The FD C → D has determinant C, which is not a super key. Thus, it violates BCNF. The highest normal form is 3NF .
subject: dbms

title: What is an RDBMS? How does it differ from a DBMS?
chunks: Feature DBMS RDBMS Data Storage Stores data as files. Stores data in tabular form (rows and columns). Relationships Does not support relationships easily. Supports complex relationships using foreign keys.
subject: dbms

title: Explain how entities and relationships of the E-R model are represented in a relational database.
chunks: Strong Entities: Represented as standalone tables. Relationships (1:N): The primary key of the '1' side is added as a foreign key to the 'N' side table. Relationships (M:N): Handled by creating a new junction table containing the primary keys of both entities.

title: Consider the relational schema Student(sid, sname), Course(cid, cname), Enrollment(sid, cid). Write relational algebra expressions.
chunks: i. Names of students enrolled in 'DBMS' π sname ( σ cname='DBMS' (Student ⨝ Enrollment ⨝ Course) ) ii. Courses where 'Alice' is enrolled π cname ( σ sname='Alice' (Course ⨝ Enrollment ⨝ Student) )

title: What are the derived operations of relational algebra? Explain Join, Intersection and Division with examples.
chunks: Derived operations are built using fundamental operations (σ, π, ×, ∪, -). Intersection (∩): Returns tuples existing in both relations. Join (⨝): A cartesian product followed by a selection. Division (÷): Used for queries involving the word "every" (e.g., students who took all courses).
subject: dbms

title: Distinguish between relational algebra and relational calculus.
chunks: Relational Algebra Relational Calculus Procedural query language. Non-procedural (declarative) query language. Specifies what data is required and how to retrieve it. Specifies what data is required without specifying how to retrieve it.
subject: dbms

title: What is the degree and cardinality of a relation?
chunks: Degree: The number of attributes (columns) in a relation. Cardinality: The number of tuples (rows) in a relation.
subject: dbms

title: What is domain relational calculus? Give an example.
chunks: Domain Relational Calculus (DRC) is a declarative query language where variables represent single attribute values (domains). Syntax: { <x1, x2, ..., xn> | P(x1, x2, ..., xn) } Example: { <N> | ∃ I, A, C ( <I, N, A, C> ∈ Student ∧ A > 20 ) }
subject: dbms

title: Explain DDL, DML, DCL and TCL commands with one example of each.
chunks: DDL: Defines structure (e.g., CREATE TABLE ). DML: Manages data (e.g., INSERT INTO ). DCL: Manages security (e.g., GRANT ). TCL: Manages transactions (e.g., COMMIT ).
subject: dbms

title: What is the use of CREATE, ALTER, DROP and TRUNCATE commands?
chunks: CREATE: Used to create new tables/objects. ALTER: Used to modify an existing table structure (add/drop columns). DROP: Deletes an entire table and its structure. TRUNCATE: Deletes all rows rapidly, but keeps the structure intact.
subject: dbms

title: Explain the DML commands INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT.
chunks: INSERT: Adds new rows. UPDATE: Modifies existing rows. DELETE: Removes specific rows. SELECT: Retrieves data from the database.
subject: dbms

title: What is the purpose of GRANT and REVOKE commands in SQL?
chunks: GRANT and REVOKE belong to the DCL (Data Control Language) category. They are used to manage database security by controlling user privileges. GRANT: Gives a user or role specific privileges on database objects. Example: GRANT SELECT ON Employees TO user_alice; REVOKE: Removes previously granted privileges. Example: REVOKE SELECT ON Employees FROM user_alice;
subject: dbms

title: Explain COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT with a suitable example.
chunks: These are TCL (Transaction Control Language) commands used to manage transactions. COMMIT: Permanently saves all changes made during the current transaction. ROLLBACK: Undoes all changes made in the current transaction. SAVEPOINT: Creates a checkpoint within a transaction to rollback to later. BEGIN; UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE id = 1; SAVEPOINT SP1; UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE id = 2; ROLLBACK TO SP1; -- Undoes the second update COMMIT; -- Permanently saves the first update
subject: dbms

title: What is a join? Explain the different types of joins, inner, left outer, right outer and full outer, with examples.
chunks: A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column. Inner Join Returns only rows with matching values in both tables. SELECT A.Name, B.Dept FROM Emp A INNER JOIN Dept B ON A.DeptID = B.DeptID; Outer Joins Left Outer: Returns all rows from the left table, and matched rows from the right. Right Outer: Returns all rows from the right table, and matched rows from the left. Full Outer: Returns all rows when there is a match in either table.
subject: dbms

title: Differentiate between an equi join and a natural join, with an example of each.
chunks: Equi Join Natural Join Explicitly uses the equality operator ( = ) in the ON clause. Implicitly matches on all columns that have the same name . No ON clause is used. Output contains duplicate matching columns. Output automatically removes duplicate matching columns. SELECT * FROM Emp JOIN Dept ON Emp.DeptID = Dept.DeptID; SELECT * FROM Emp NATURAL JOIN Dept;
subject: dbms

title: What is a self join? What is a cross join? Explain with examples.
chunks: Self Join A table is joined with itself using aliases. SELECT E.Name AS Employee, M.Name AS Manager FROM Employee E JOIN Employee M ON E.ManagerID = M.EmpID; Cross Join Produces the Cartesian Product of two tables (every row matched with every row). SELECT T.Name, C.RoomNo FROM Teachers T CROSS JOIN Classrooms C;
subject: dbms

title: Explain the aggregate functions available in SQL, COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN, giving an example of each.
chunks: Aggregate functions perform a calculation on a set of values and return a single summarizing value. COUNT(): Returns the number of rows. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Employees; SUM(): Returns the total sum of a column. SELECT SUM(Salary) FROM Employees; AVG(): Returns the average value. SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employees; MAX() / MIN(): Returns the largest / smallest value. SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees;
subject: dbms

title: What is the purpose of the GROUP BY clause? Explain with a suitable query.
chunks: The GROUP BY clause is used to arrange identical data into groups. It is typically used in conjunction with aggregate functions (COUNT, MAX, MIN, SUM, AVG). Scenario: Find the total number of employees in each department. SELECT DeptID, COUNT(EmpID) AS TotalEmployees FROM Employee GROUP BY DeptID;
subject: dbms

title: How is the HAVING clause different from the WHERE clause? Justify with an example.
chunks: WHERE Clause HAVING Clause Filters individual rows before grouping. Filters groups after grouping. Cannot contain aggregate functions. Can contain aggregate functions. Example SELECT DeptID, AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE HireDate > '2020-01-01' -- Filters rows first GROUP BY DeptID HAVING AVG(Salary) > 50000; -- Filters groups
subject: dbms

title: Explain the use of the ORDER BY clause with an example.
chunks: The ORDER BY clause is used to sort the result set of a query in either ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order. Example: SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee ORDER BY Salary DESC;
subject: dbms

title: What are nested queries? Why are they used? Explain with a suitable example.
chunks: A nested query (subquery) is a query embedded within another query. They are used to break down complex queries into isolated steps. Scenario: Find employees who earn a salary greater than the average salary. SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee);
subject: dbms

title: What is a correlated subquery? How is it different from a simple subquery?
chunks: Simple Subquery Correlated Subquery Executes completely independent of the outer query. Depends on the outer query for its values. Executes exactly once for the entire outer query. Executes repeatedly , once for every row processed by the outer query. Example (Correlated) SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee E1 WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee E2 WHERE E1.DeptID = E2.DeptID);
subject: dbms

title: Explain the use of IN, EXISTS, ANY and ALL operators in a nested query.
chunks: IN: Checks if a value matches any value in a list or subquery result. WHERE DeptID IN (SELECT DeptID FROM Departments) EXISTS: Evaluates to TRUE if the subquery returns one or more records. WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Orders.CustID = Customers.ID) ANY (or SOME): Compares a value to each value in a list and evaluates to TRUE if any comparison is true. WHERE Salary > ANY (SELECT Salary FROM IT_Dept) ALL: Evaluates to TRUE only if the comparison is true for all values in the list. WHERE Salary > ALL (SELECT Salary FROM Interns)
subject: dbms

title: What is a view? What are its advantages?
chunks: A View is a virtual table based on the result-set of an SQL statement. It contains rows and columns, just like a real table, but holds no data of its own. Advantages Security: Restricts access to specific rows/columns of a table. Simplicity: Hides complex joins and calculations into a single virtual table. Data Independence: Insulates applications from changes in base table structures.
subject: dbms

title: Differentiate between a simple view and a materialized view.
chunks: Simple View Materialized View Virtual table; does not store data physically. Stores the actual result data physically on disk. Query is executed every time the view is accessed. Data is pre-computed, providing much faster read access. Always shows up-to-date real-time data. Needs to be refreshed periodically to show updated data.
subject: dbms

title: Can every view be updated? Explain the limitations of an updatable view with an example.
chunks: No , not all views can be updated. A view is updatable only if the DBMS can unambiguously trace the update back to the underlying base table rows. Limitations (Cannot Update If:) It contains aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX). It contains GROUP BY or HAVING clauses. It is built using multiple tables (Joins), depending on the DBMS. It uses the DISTINCT keyword. Example A view CREATE VIEW Dept_Salaries AS SELECT DeptID, AVG(Salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY DeptID; cannot be updated because an update to an average salary cannot be mapped to individual employees.
subject: dbms

title: Explain generalization, specialization and aggregation in the Extended E-R model.
chunks: Specialization (Top-Down) The process of defining a set of subclasses from an entity type based on distinguishing characteristics. Example: An Employee can be specialized into Hourly_Emp and Salaried_Emp . Generalization (Bottom-Up) The reverse of specialization. Extracting shared characteristics from multiple entity types to create a generalized superclass. Example: Car and Truck generalized into Vehicle . Aggregation Treating a relationship between entities as a single abstract entity, allowing relationships to participate in other relationships. Example: A Project and Employee have a Works_On relationship. A Manager manages the entire Works_On relationship, treating it as one aggregated entity.
subject: dbms

title: What is decomposition? Explain the concepts of lossless-join and dependency-preserving decomposition.
chunks: Decomposition is the process of breaking down a large, poorly-designed relation into two or more smaller relations to eliminate redundancy and anomalies. Lossless-Join Decomposition A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if joining R1 and R2 back together using a Natural Join yields the exact original relation R, without generating spurious (fake) tuples. Condition: The common attributes must be a candidate key for at least one of the decomposed relations (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2 ). Dependency-Preserving Decomposition A decomposition is dependency-preserving if all original functional dependencies can be checked and enforced using only the decomposed relations, without needing to join them back together.
subject: dbms

title: How is decomposition related to normalization? Explain with a small example.
chunks: Normalization uses Decomposition as its primary mechanism. When a relation violates a normal form, we decompose it into smaller relations that satisfy the normal form. Example Suppose a relation R(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID → EmpName, DeptID and DeptID → DeptName . This violates 3NF due to the transitive dependency ( EmpID → DeptID → DeptName ). Normalization Process: We decompose R into two relations to remove the redundancy: 1. Employee(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID) 2. Department(DeptID, DeptName) This decomposition is both lossless-join (because DeptID is a primary key in Department) and dependency-preserving.
subject: dbms

title: Compare relational algebra with SQL as two different ways of expressing the same query.
chunks: Feature Relational Algebra SQL Nature Theoretical, mathematical foundation. Procedural. Practical, commercial language. Declarative. Selection (Rows) σ condition (Table) WHERE condition Projection (Columns) π col1, col2 (Table) SELECT col1, col2 Joins Table1 ⨝ Table2 Table1 JOIN Table2 Duplicates Automatically removes duplicates (set semantics). Retains duplicates by default (bag semantics); requires DISTINCT to remove.
subject: dbms

title: Write a query to display the names of students who are enrolled in the course 'DBMS'.

SELECT s.sname FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid WHERE c.cname = 'DBMS'; Alternative (Using Subqueries) SELECT sname FROM Student WHERE sid IN ( SELECT sid FROM Enrollment WHERE cid IN ( SELECT cid FROM Course WHERE cname = 'DBMS' ) );

title: Write a query to display, course-wise, how many students have enrolled in each course.

title: Write a query using HAVING to display students who are enrolled in more than 3 courses.

title: Write a query to display the student name along with the names of the courses they have opted for, using a suitable join.

title: Write a query to find students who have not enrolled in any course so far.
chunks: Using LEFT JOIN SELECT s.sname FROM Student s LEFT JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid WHERE e.cid IS NULL; Using NOT EXISTS SELECT sname FROM Student s WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Enrollment e WHERE e.sid = s.sid );

title: Write a nested query to find the student(s) who scored the highest marks in the course 'DBMS'.
chunks: Assuming Enrollment(sid, cid, marks) . SELECT s.sname, e.marks FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid WHERE c.cname = 'DBMS' AND e.marks = ( SELECT MAX(e2.marks) FROM Enrollment e2 JOIN Course c2 ON e2.cid = c2.cid WHERE c2.cname = 'DBMS' );
subject: dbms

title: Create a view that shows the student name, course name and marks for every enrollment record.
chunks: CREATE VIEW Student_Grades AS SELECT s.sname, c.cname, e.marks FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid; You can then query this view like a regular table: SELECT * FROM Student_Grades;
