title: Write a relational algebra expression to retrieve the names of students enrolled in the course 'DBMS'.
chunks: Relational Algebra: π sname ( Student ⨝ Enrollment ⨝ σ cname='DBMS' (Course) ) Breakdown: Select only the course where cname is 'DBMS' (σ). Natural Join (⨝) the result with Enrollment and Student. Project (π) only the student name (sname).
subject: dbms

title: Using the division operation of relational algebra, write an expression to find students who are enrolled in every course offered.
chunks: The division operator ( ÷ ) is used specifically for queries involving "every" or "all". Expression: π sid (Enrollment) ÷ π cid (Course) To get the student names, we natural join this result with the Student table: π sname ( Student ⨝ (π sid, cid (Enrollment) ÷ π cid (Course)) )

title: Write a correlated subquery to list students who have scored more than the average marks obtained in their respective course.
chunks: SELECT s.sname, e1.cid, e1.marks FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e1 ON s.sid = e1.sid WHERE e1.marks > ( SELECT AVG(e2.marks) FROM Enrollment e2 WHERE e1.cid = e2.cid ); The inner query recalculates the average marks dynamically for every row of the outer query, matching the cid .

title: What is the use of CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE commands? Why are DDL statements said to be auto-committed?
chunks: CREATE TABLE is used to create a new table in the database. ALTER TABLE is used to add, delete, or modify columns in an existing table. DROP TABLE is used to delete an existing table completely (including its structure and data). DDL statements are auto-committed because they alter the database schema directly and cannot be rolled back in most RDBMS like MySQL and Oracle.
subject: dbms

title: Write a CREATE TABLE statement for a Library_Book table having Book_ID, Title, Author, Price and Published_Date, choosing appropriate data types.
chunks: CREATE TABLE Library_Book ( Book_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Title VARCHAR(100), Author VARCHAR(50), Price DECIMAL(8,2), Published_Date DATE );

chunks: ALTER TABLE Student ADD Email VARCHAR(40);

title: Give the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP commands.
chunks: DELETE is a DML command used to remove specific rows based on a WHERE clause. It can be rolled back. TRUNCATE is a DDL command that removes all rows from a table quickly by deallocating the pages. It cannot be rolled back and resets identity columns. DROP is a DDL command that completely deletes the table structure and its data from the database.
subject: dbms

title: Explain the five constraints NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK, giving an example of each.
chunks: NOT NULL : Ensures a column cannot have a NULL value. Ex: Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE : Ensures all values in a column are distinct. Ex: Email VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE PRIMARY KEY : Uniquely identifies each record. It is NOT NULL + UNIQUE. Ex: ID INT PRIMARY KEY FOREIGN KEY : Ensures referential integrity by linking to a primary key in another table. Ex: FOREIGN KEY (DeptID) REFERENCES Dept(ID) CHECK : Ensures values in a column satisfy a specific condition. Ex: Age INT CHECK (Age >= 18)
subject: dbms

title: What is the difference between a column-level and a table-level constraint? When is a table-level constraint compulsory?
chunks: Column-level constraints are defined immediately after the data type of a column. Table-level constraints are defined at the end of the table creation and can span multiple columns. A table-level constraint is compulsory when defining a composite key (a constraint that involves more than one column).
subject: dbms

title: Write a CREATE TABLE statement for Department(Dept_ID, Dept_Name), keeping Dept_ID as the primary key.
chunks: CREATE TABLE Department ( Dept_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Dept_Name VARCHAR(50) );
subject: dbms

title: Write a CREATE TABLE statement for Employee(Emp_ID, Name, Email, Dept_ID, Salary), where Emp_ID is the primary key, Name cannot be left blank and Email must be unique.
chunks: CREATE TABLE Employee ( Emp_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Email VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE, Dept_ID INT, Salary DECIMAL(10,2) );
subject: dbms

title: Using ALTER TABLE, add a foreign key on Employee.Dept_ID referencing Department.Dept_ID.
chunks: ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT fk_dept FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(Dept_ID);
subject: dbms

title: Using ALTER TABLE, put a check constraint on the Employee table so that Salary is always greater than zero.
chunks: ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT chk_salary CHECK (Salary > 0);
subject: dbms

title: A table can have more than one UNIQUE constraint but only one PRIMARY KEY. Justify why this is so.
chunks: A Primary Key is strictly designed to be the single, definitive row identifier used by the database engine to organize and index the physical storage (e.g. clustered index). There can only be one physical ordering. However, multiple columns may have naturally unique data (like an Email or Phone number), which is why multiple UNIQUE constraints are permitted to enforce business rules.
subject: dbms

title: Explain the numeric functions ROUND, TRUNCATE, CEIL, FLOOR, ABS, MOD, POWER and SQRT, giving an example of each.
chunks: ROUND(n, d) : Rounds n to d decimal places. ROUND(3.456, 2) → 3.46 TRUNCATE(n, d) : Cuts off n at d decimal places without rounding. TRUNCATE(3.456, 2) → 3.45 CEIL(n) : Returns the smallest integer ≥ n . CEIL(3.14) → 4 FLOOR(n) : Returns the largest integer ≤ n . FLOOR(3.8) → 3 ABS(n) : Returns the absolute (positive) value. ABS(-5) → 5 MOD(x, y) : Returns the remainder of x/y. MOD(10, 3) → 1 POWER(x, y) : Returns x raised to power y. POWER(2, 3) → 8 SQRT(n) : Returns the square root. SQRT(16) → 4

title: Round off 78.3456 to 2 decimal places using ROUND, and also truncate it to 2 decimal places using TRUNCATE. Why do the two results come out different?
chunks: SELECT ROUND(78.3456, 2); -- Result: 78.35 SELECT TRUNCATE(78.3456, 2); -- Result: 78.34 Reason : ROUND evaluates the third decimal digit (5) and mathematically rounds up. TRUNCATE simply drops all digits after the 2nd decimal place without any mathematical evaluation.

Ex: SELECT DATEDIFF('2023-10-10', '2023-10-01'); → 9 DATE_ADD(date, INTERVAL expr unit) : Adds a time interval to a date. Ex: SELECT DATE_ADD('2023-01-01', INTERVAL 5 DAY); DATE_FORMAT(date, format) : Formats a date string. Ex: SELECT DATE_FORMAT(CURDATE(), '%Y-%m-%d');

chunks: CONCAT(s1, s2) : Joins two or more strings. Ex: CONCAT('Data', 'base') → 'Database' UPPER(s) / LOWER(s) : Converts a string to all uppercase or lowercase. Ex: UPPER('sql') → 'SQL' LENGTH(s) : Returns the number of characters in a string. Ex: LENGTH('DBMS') → 4 SUBSTRING(s, start, len) : Extracts a part of a string. Ex: SUBSTRING('Database', 1, 4) → 'Data' TRIM(s) : Removes leading and trailing spaces. Ex: TRIM(' SQL ') → 'SQL' REPLACE(s, old, new) : Replaces all occurrences of a substring. title: Explain UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT and MINUS/EXCEPT with an example of each. What condition must both the SELECT statements satisfy before these operators can be applied?
chunks: Set Operators: UNION : Combines results of two queries, removing duplicates. UNION ALL : Combines results of two queries, keeping all duplicates. INTERSECT : Returns only the rows that appear in both queries. MINUS / EXCEPT : Returns rows from the first query that are not present in the second. Condition for application (Union Compatibility): Both SELECT statements must have the same number of columns. The corresponding columns must have compatible data types in the same order.

title: What is a transaction? Explain the ACID properties with the help of a bank transfer example.
chunks: A transaction is a logical unit of work consisting of one or more SQL statements that must be executed entirely or not at all. ACID Properties (Bank Transfer Example: A to B): Atomicity : "All or nothing." If money is deducted from A, it MUST be credited to B. If either fails, the entire transaction is rolled back. Consistency : The database must remain in a valid state. The total sum of A + B's balances must be the same before and after the transaction. Isolation : Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. If another transaction reads A's balance during the transfer, it will see the state either strictly before or strictly after, not midway. Durability : Once the transaction is committed, the changes are permanent and will survive system crashes. Transaction State Diagram
subject: dbms

title: Explain COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT with a suitable example on the ACCOUNT table.
chunks: COMMIT : Saves all changes made during the current transaction permanently. ROLLBACK : Undoes all changes made during the current transaction, reverting to the last commit. SAVEPOINT : Sets a marker within a transaction so you can roll back to that specific point without canceling the entire transaction. START TRANSACTION; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A101'; SAVEPOINT step1; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; -- If something goes wrong here: ROLLBACK TO step1; -- Undoes only the A102 update COMMIT; -- Saves the final state
subject: dbms

title: Write a transaction that transfers Rs. 3000 from account A102 to account A103, placing a SAVEPOINT just before the transfer, and finally commit it.
chunks: START TRANSACTION; SAVEPOINT before_transfer; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A103'; COMMIT;

title: In one or two lines each, state the purpose of a stored procedure, a sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL), a cursor and a trigger.
chunks: Stored Procedure : A pre-compiled collection of SQL statements saved in the database that can be executed as a single callable routine. Sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT) : Automatically generates unique, sequential numeric values, typically used for primary keys. Cursor : A database object used to retrieve and process rows one by one from a result set inside a stored procedure. Trigger : A special type of stored procedure that automatically executes (fires) in response to specific DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a table.
subject: dbms

title: What is the difference between a BEFORE trigger and an AFTER trigger? What do the keywords NEW and OLD refer to inside a trigger?
chunks: BEFORE Trigger executes before the triggering DML operation is applied (useful for validation/modification of incoming data). AFTER Trigger executes after the operation (useful for auditing or cascading changes to other tables). NEW refers to the incoming data (being inserted or updated). OLD refers to the existing data in the table before the operation (being updated or deleted).
subject: dbms

title: What is the purpose of exception handling in a stored procedure? Briefly explain DECLARE ... HANDLER and the SIGNAL statement.
chunks: Exception handling ensures that if an error occurs during execution, the stored procedure can catch it and gracefully handle it (e.g., rolling back a transaction) instead of crashing. DECLARE ... HANDLER : Defines a block of code to execute when a specific error or condition occurs (e.g., DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION ). SIGNAL : Used to artificially raise a custom error or exception, returning a custom SQLSTATE and message to the caller.
subject: dbms

Unit I: Intro & ER DBMS

Definition A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that interacts with end-users, applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze data. It allows users to create, read, update, and delete data in a database. Advantages over File-Processing Data Redundancy and Inconsistency: Centralizes data, eliminating duplicate files and ensuring updates propagate everywhere. Data Isolation: Applications do not need to know the physical structure of the data files. Integrity Problems: Allows defining explicit integrity constraints (e.g., account balance > 0). Security Problems: Offers fine-grained access control and user authorization. Concurrent Access: Manages simultaneous access securely, preventing anomalies. Data redundancy and data inconsistency

Definitions Data Redundancy: The unnecessary duplication of data in a database. (e.g., storing a student's address in both the Library and Department files). Data Inconsistency: A consequence of redundancy where different copies of the same data hold different values (e.g., address updated in Library but not Department). DBMS Solution A DBMS minimizes redundancy by storing a single, centralized copy of the data (Data Normalization). Because there is only one authoritative copy, inconsistency is inherently prevented. Give the difference between a database system and a file-based system

Differences Structure: DB systems store data in structured formats (tables/graphs); File systems store data in plain text/binary files. Data Independence: DB systems separate applications from data structure; File systems tightly couple applications to file formats. Querying: DB systems provide robust query languages (SQL); File systems require custom application code to extract data. Draw and explain the three-level (ANSI-SPARC) architecture of a DBMS

The Three Levels External Level (View Level): The highest level, describing only the part of the database relevant to a specific user group (hiding the rest). Conceptual Level (Logical Level): Describes what data is stored in the entire database and the relationships among those data. Used by DBAs. Internal Level (Physical Level): Describes exactly how the data is physically stored on disk (data structures, file organizations). Exam Tip: The primary objective of this architecture is to achieve Data Independence . Data abstraction

Definition Data abstraction is the process of hiding complex internal data structures and storage details from the user, presenting only a simplified, usable view of the data. Three Levels Physical Level: Hides the complexity of block structures, indexing, and bytes on disk. Logical Level: Hides physical storage but reveals entities, data types, and relationships. Developers interact here. View Level: Hides the entire logical schema except for specific fields the end-user is authorized to see (e.g., a teller seeing only names and balances). Terms schema and instance

Definition Schema: The overall logical design/blueprint of the database. It changes rarely. Instance: The snapshot of data residing in the database at a specific moment in time. It changes frequently. Importance This distinction is crucial for maintaining data independence—altering the schema (like adding a column) should not arbitrarily destroy the existing instances. Data independence

Definition Data independence is the ability to modify a schema definition in one level without affecting a schema definition in the next higher level. Types Physical Data Independence: Ability to modify the internal/physical schema without altering the conceptual schema. Example: Changing a file from sequential to a B+ tree index to improve performance; application code doesn't change. Logical Data Independence: Ability to modify the conceptual schema without altering the external schema (user views). Example: Splitting an Employee table into two normalized tables; the original view can be maintained using a SQL JOIN, shielding the frontend application. Who are the different types of database users

Types of Users Parametric (Naive) Users: End-users who interact via standard GUI applications without knowing SQL (e.g., Bank Tellers). Application Programmers: Software engineers who write the backend logic connecting to the DB. Sophisticated Users: Analysts who interact directly with the DB using SQL queries to generate reports. Database Administrators (DBA): IT professionals who manage security, schemas, and performance tuning. List the responsibilities of a Database Administrator (DBA)

Responsibilities Schema definition and modification. Defining storage structures and access methods (indexing). Granting user authority and managing access security. Routine maintenance, database backups, and performance monitoring. Hierarchical, network, relational and object-oriented data models

Comparison Hierarchical: Data organized in a tree structure (1:N relationships). Fast but inflexible; requires navigating rigid pointers. Network: Data organized in a graph (M:N relationships allowed). Highly complex and difficult to maintain. Relational: Data organized in 2D tables (relations). Uses declarative SQL. Extremely flexible and mathematically sound. Object-Oriented: Data stored as objects with methods, matching OOP languages. Best for complex data (e.g., CAD/CAM). Most Widely Used The Relational Model is most widely used today due to its simplicity, robust theoretical foundation (normalization), and standard interface (SQL) which provides unparalleled data independence. Advantages of the relational model over the other data models

Advantages Simplicity: Uses a simple tabular structure (rows and columns) that is easy to understand compared to complex graph/tree pointers. Flexibility: Supports ad-hoc querying using standard SQL. Data Independence: Strong separation between logical representation and physical storage. Terms super key, candidate key, primary key and foreign key

Explanation Super Key: Any combination of columns that uniquely identifies a row. (e.g., StudentID + Name ) Candidate Key: A minimal super key; it uniquely identifies a row with no unnecessary columns. (e.g., StudentID or Email ) Primary Key: The specific candidate key chosen to identify rows. Cannot be NULL. (e.g., StudentID ) Foreign Key: A column that refers to the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity. (e.g., Dept_ID in a Student table referencing the Department table) Integrity constraints in a relational model

Definition Integrity constraints are rules applied to a database to ensure the data is accurate, consistent, and valid. The Four Constraints Domain Constraint: Restricts the values a column can hold to a valid set (e.g., Age must be a positive integer). Key Constraint: Ensures that candidate/primary keys are completely unique for every row. Entity Integrity: States that no part of a Primary Key can be NULL, because a NULL value cannot uniquely identify a row. Referential Integrity: States that if a foreign key exists in a relation, its value must either match a primary key value in the referenced relation or be NULL. (e.g., You cannot enroll a student in a non-existent Course_ID). E-R model

Definition The Entity-Relationship (E-R) model is a high-level conceptual data model that visually represents entities (objects) and the relationships between them. Notations Rectangle: Entity sets Ellipse: Attributes Diamond: Relationship sets Lines: Link attributes to entities and entities to relationships Entity, entity set, attribute and relationship, and illustrate each

Definitions Entity: A real-world object with independent existence (e.g., a specific student). Entity Set: A collection of similar entities (e.g., all Students). Attribute: A property describing an entity (e.g., Name, Age). Relationship: An association among two or more entities (e.g., Student Enroll Course). Different types of attributes, simple, composite, derived, multivalued and key attribute,

Attribute Types Simple: Indivisible atomic values (e.g., Gender ). Composite: Can be broken down into sub-parts (e.g., Name into First Name, Last Name). Derived: Calculated from other attributes; not physically stored (e.g., Age derived from DOB). Multivalued: Can hold multiple values for a single entity (e.g., Phone_Numbers ). Key: Uniquely identifies the entity (e.g., Roll_No ). Different types of relationships that can exist between two entities

Cardinality Ratios One-to-One (1:1): One entity in A is associated with at most one in B. (e.g., Department 1:1 Manager). One-to-Many (1:N): One entity in A is associated with many in B. (e.g., Department 1:N Employees). Many-to-Many (M:N): Many entities in A associated with many in B. (e.g., Student M:N Course). Weak entity set

Definition A weak entity set lacks sufficient attributes to form a primary key. It depends on a strong entity (identifying owner) and uses the owner's key plus its own partial key to identify rows. Example A Dependent (spouse/child) of an Employee. The dependent is identified by combining their Name (partial key) with the owner's Employee ID. Unary, binary and ternary relationships

Degrees of Relationships Unary (Degree 1): Relationship between instances of a single entity set (e.g., Employee Manages Employee). Binary (Degree 2): Relationship between two entity sets (e.g., Student Takes Course). Ternary (Degree 3): Relationship connecting three entity sets simultaneously (e.g., Supplier Supplies Part To Project). Exam Tip: A ternary relationship is not just three binary relationships; it represents a single fact involving all three entities together. Total participation and partial participation constraints in an E-R diagram

Differentiation Total Participation (Mandatory): Every entity MUST participate in at least one relationship. Indicated by a double line. (e.g., Every Employee must belong to a Department). Partial Participation (Optional): Only some entities may participate. Indicated by a single line. (e.g., Only some Employees are Managers of a Department). Generalization and specialization in the Extended E-R model

Specialization (Top-Down) The process of defining a set of subclasses from a single entity type (the superclass). It involves identifying characteristics that distinguish some entities in the set from others. Example: An Employee superclass can be specialized into Engineer , Manager , and Technician subclasses based on job role. Generalization (Bottom-Up) The reverse process of specialization. Multiple entity types with common attributes are synthesized into a single, generalized superclass. Example: Car and Truck entities share attributes like Vehicle_ID and Price, so they can be generalized into a Vehicle superclass. Overlapping and disjoint specialization

Disjoint Specialization An entity can be a member of at most one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by a 'd' in the circle. Example: An Employee can be either an Hourly_Employee or a Salaried_Employee , but never both at the same time. Overlapping Specialization An entity may be a member of more than one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by an 'o' in the circle. Example: A Person can simultaneously be an Alumnus and an Employee of a university. Aggregation in E-R modelling

Definition Aggregation is an abstraction where a relationship set (and its associated entities) is treated as a higher-level entity set. When is it required? The basic E-R model cannot express relationships among relationships. Aggregation is required when a relationship between two entities needs to participate in another relationship with a third entity. Example Consider Employee working on a Project . This forms the relationship Works_On . If we want to record the Manager who oversees this specific (Employee-Project) assignment, we aggregate Works_On into a single entity, and create a new relationship Manages between it and Manager . Mapping cardinality

Definition Mapping cardinality (or cardinality ratio) expresses the number of entities to which another entity can be associated via a relationship set. Types One-to-One (1:1): An entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B, and vice versa. One-to-Many (1:N): An entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B. An entity in B is associated with at most one entity in A. Many-to-One (N:1): An entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B. An entity in B is associated with any number of entities in A. Many-to-Many (M:N): An entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B, and vice versa. Functional dependency

Definition A functional dependency (FD) is a constraint between two sets of attributes in a relation. If A → B (A determines B), then for every valid instance of the relation, any two tuples that agree on the attribute A must also agree on the attribute B. Importance Functional dependencies are the theoretical bedrock of Normalization . They are used to specify constraints on data, discover candidate keys, and decompose relations to eliminate redundancy and update anomalies. Insertion, deletion and update anomalies

The Three Anomalies Update Anomaly: If data is stored redundantly, changing it in one row requires changing it in all rows. Missing one causes inconsistency (e.g., changing a department's location). Insertion Anomaly: The inability to add data to the database due to absence of other data (e.g., unable to add a new Department because it has no Employees yet, and Employee_ID is the primary key). Deletion Anomaly: The unintended loss of data when deleting a row (e.g., deleting the only employee in a department also deletes the department's information). How Normalization Helps Normalization resolves these by decomposing large, poorly structured tables into smaller, well-structured tables where each table represents a single logical theme or entity. By linking them with foreign keys, redundancy is eliminated, which inherently solves update, insertion, and deletion anomalies. Normalization

Definition Normalization is the process of organizing data to minimize redundancy and eliminate anomalies by dividing larger tables into smaller tables and defining relationships between them using functional dependencies. The Normal Forms First Normal Form (1NF): All attributes must be atomic (indivisible). No repeating groups or arrays allowed in a cell. Second Normal Form (2NF): Must be in 1NF, and all non-key attributes must be fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key. (Eliminates partial dependencies). Third Normal Form (3NF): Must be in 2NF, and no non-key attribute can be dependent on another non-key attribute. (Eliminates transitive dependencies: X → Y and Y → Z). BCNF

Definition Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X must be a super key. It is a stronger, stricter version of 3NF. Difference from 3NF 3NF allows a dependency X → Y where X is NOT a super key, provided that Y is a prime attribute (part of a candidate key). BCNF does not allow this exception. A table can be in 3NF but fail BCNF if it has overlapping candidate keys. Example Consider Relation(Student, Course, Instructor) . Keys are (Student, Course) and (Student, Instructor). FD: Instructor → Course . It is in 3NF because Course is a prime attribute. However, it violates BCNF because Instructor is not a super key. Write a short note on 4NF and 5NF,

Fourth Normal Form (4NF) Deals with Multi-valued Dependencies (MVD) . A table is in 4NF if it is in BCNF and contains no non-trivial multi-valued dependencies (where one attribute determines a set of values for another, independent of a third). Example: An Employee has multiple Skills and multiple Dependents. Storing them in one table creates massive redundancy. We split into (Emp, Skill) and (Emp, Dependent) . Fifth Normal Form (5NF) Deals with Join Dependencies . Also known as Project-Join Normal Form (PJNF). A table is in 5NF if it is in 4NF and cannot be decomposed into smaller tables without losing data (lossless join). It ensures that all join dependencies are implied by candidate keys. Lossless-join decomposition

Definition Lossless-join decomposition means that if a relation R is decomposed into R1 and R2, joining them back together via a Natural Join will yield the exact original relation R, without any missing rows (loss of data) or extra spurious rows (creation of invalid data). Condition The decomposition is lossless if the common attribute(s) between R1 and R2 form a super key for either R1 or R2. (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 OR R1 ∩ R2 → R2). Example Splitting Employee(ID, Name, Dept, Dept_Location) into Emp(ID, Name, Dept) and Department(Dept, Dept_Location) is lossless because their intersection, Dept , is a primary key for the Department table. Dependency-preserving decomposition and give a suitable example

Definition A decomposition is dependency-preserving if the union of the functional dependencies in the decomposed relations logically implies all the functional dependencies of the original relation. This ensures that updates can be checked for validity without joining the tables back together. Example Original Relation: R(A, B, C) Functional Dependencies (FDs): A → B, B → C Decomposition: R1(A, B) and R2(B, C). FDs in R1: A → B. FDs in R2: B → C. Since (A → B) ∪ (B → C) covers all original FDs, it is a dependency-preserving decomposition . Identifying Partial Dependencies Suppose the relation is R(StudentID, SubjectID, StudentName, Grade) . The primary key is (StudentID, SubjectID) . StudentID → StudentName (StudentName depends only on part of the key) — Partial Dependency StudentID, SubjectID → Grade (Grade depends on the whole key) — Full Dependency Decomposition into 2NF We split the table to remove the partial dependency: Student ( StudentID , StudentName) Enrollment ( StudentID, SubjectID , Grade) Both tables are now in 2NF as all non-prime attributes fully depend on their respective primary keys. Table below has EmployeeID as its primary key

Violation of 3NF Consider Employee(EmpID, Name, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID is the primary key. Functional Dependencies: 1. EmpID → DeptID 2. DeptID → DeptName Because EmpID → DeptName through DeptID , this is a Transitive Dependency . 3NF forbids non-prime attributes depending on other non-prime attributes. Decomposition into 3NF We decompose the relation to separate the department details: Employee ( EmpID , Name, DeptID ) Department ( DeptID , DeptName) In the table below, each mentor teaches only one subject

Checking BCNF Relation: R(StudentID, Subject, Mentor) FDs: {StudentID, Subject} → Mentor , and Mentor → Subject (each mentor teaches one subject). Because Mentor → Subject exists, but Mentor is not a super key , the table violates BCNF (even though it is in 3NF since Subject is a prime attribute). BCNF Decomposition We must pull the violating determinant out into its own table: Mentor_Subject ( Mentor , Subject) Student_Mentor ( StudentID, Mentor ) Now all determinants are candidate keys. Table below stores a student's hobbies and the languages they know together, forcing every combination to be listed

Violation of 4NF Relation: R(StudentID, Hobby, Language) A student's hobbies are completely independent of the languages they speak. This creates two Multi-Valued Dependencies (MVDs) : StudentID ⟶ Hobby and StudentID ⟶ Language . Storing them together forces a Cartesian product (e.g., 2 hobbies × 3 languages = 6 rows for one student). Since 4NF forbids non-trivial MVDs, this violates 4NF. 4NF Decomposition Split into two tables to eliminate the Cartesian product: Student_Hobby ( StudentID, Hobby ) Student_Language ( StudentID, Language ) Given a relation R(A, B, C, D, E)

Computing {A, C} + Start with the base set: {A, C} Using A → B , add B. The set becomes {A, B, C} Using BC → D (we have both B and C), add D. The set becomes {A, B, C, D} Using D → E , add E. The set becomes {A, B, C, D, E} Conclusion Since the closure of {A, C} contains all the attributes of the relation R, {A, C} is a super key . Assuming no proper subset of {A, C} can determine all attributes, {A, C} is a Candidate Key . Consider the relation Student_Course(Roll_No, Course_ID, Course_Name, Instructor)

Analysis Primary Key: (Roll_No, Course_ID) The FD Course_ID → Course_Name is a Partial Dependency because Course_Name depends only on a part of the primary key (Course_ID), violating 2NF. 2NF Decomposition Course ( Course_ID , Course_Name) Student_Course ( Roll_No, Course_ID , Instructor) Now, both relations are in 2NF. Consider the relation Employee(Emp_ID, Emp_Name, Dept_ID, Dept_Name, Dept_Location)

Analysis Primary Key: Emp_ID . Since the key is a single attribute, there are no partial dependencies, so it is in 2NF . However, the FD Dept_ID → Dept_Name, Dept_Location creates a Transitive Dependency (Emp_ID → Dept_ID → Dept_Name). This violates 3NF. 3NF Decomposition Employee ( Emp_ID , Emp_Name, Dept_ID ) Department ( Dept_ID , Dept_Name, Dept_Location) Consider the relation R(Student, Subject, Teacher)

Analysis Candidate Keys: (Student, Subject) and (Student, Teacher) . For the FD Teacher → Subject , Teacher is a determinant but not a super key . Therefore, R violates BCNF. BCNF Decomposition Teach_Subj ( Teacher , Subject) Stud_Teach ( Student, Teacher ) Both tables are now strictly in BCNF. Given a relation R(A, B, C, D)

Candidate Keys {A, B} + = {A, B, C, D} {B, C} + = {A, B, C, D} (since C → D and D → A) {B, D} + = {A, B, C, D} (since D → A and AB → C) The candidate keys are AB, BC, and BD . All attributes are prime attributes except none (every attribute is part of at least one candidate key). Highest Normal Form Because there are no non-prime attributes, the relation is automatically in 3NF . However, check BCNF: The FD C → D has determinant C, which is not a super key. Thus, it violates BCNF. The highest normal form is 3NF .

Unit II: Relational Algebra & SQL RDBMS Feature DBMS RDBMS Data Storage Stores data as files. Stores data in tabular form (rows and columns). Relationships Does not support relationships easily. Supports complex relationships using foreign keys. Entities and relationships of the E-R model are represented in a relational database Strong Entities: Represented as standalone tables. Relationships (1:N): The primary key of the '1' side is added as a foreign key to the 'N' side table. Relationships (M:N): Handled by creating a new junction table containing the primary keys of both entities. Consider the relational schema Student(sid, sname), Course(cid, cname), Enrollment(sid, cid)

i. Names of students enrolled in 'DBMS' π sname ( σ cname='DBMS' (Student ⨝ Enrollment ⨝ Course) ) ii. Courses where 'Alice' is enrolled π cname ( σ sname='Alice' (Course ⨝ Enrollment ⨝ Student) ) Derived operations of relational algebra Derived operations are built using fundamental operations (σ, π, ×, ∪, -). Intersection (∩): Returns tuples existing in both relations. Join (⨝): A cartesian product followed by a selection. Division (÷): Used for queries involving the word "every" (e.g., students who took all courses). Relational algebra and relational calculus Relational Algebra Relational Calculus Procedural query language. Non-procedural (declarative) query language. Specifies what data is required and how to retrieve it. Specifies what data is required without specifying how to retrieve it. Degree and cardinality of a relation Degree: The number of attributes (columns) in a relation. Cardinality: The number of tuples (rows) in a relation. Domain relational calculus Domain Relational Calculus (DRC) is a declarative query language where variables represent single attribute values (domains). Syntax: { <x1, x2, ..., xn> | P(x1, x2, ..., xn) } Example: { <N> | ∃ I, A, C ( <I, N, A, C> ∈ Student ∧ A > 20 ) } DDL, DML, DCL

and TCL commands DDL: Defines structure (e.g., CREATE TABLE ). DML: Manages data (e.g., INSERT INTO ). DCL: Manages security (e.g., GRANT ). TCL: Manages transactions (e.g., COMMIT ). Use of CREATE, ALTER, DROP and TRUNCATE commands CREATE: Used to create new tables/objects. ALTER: Used to modify an existing table structure (add/drop columns). DROP: Deletes an entire table and its structure. TRUNCATE: Deletes all rows rapidly, but keeps the structure intact. DML commands INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT INSERT: Adds new rows. UPDATE: Modifies existing rows. DELETE: Removes specific rows. SELECT: Retrieves data from the database. Purpose of GRANT and REVOKE commands in SQL GRANT and REVOKE belong to the DCL (Data Control Language) category. They are used to manage database security by controlling user privileges. GRANT: Gives a user or role specific privileges on database objects. Example: GRANT SELECT ON Employees TO user_alice; REVOKE: Removes previously granted privileges. Example: REVOKE SELECT ON Employees FROM user_alice; COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT These are TCL (Transaction Control Language) commands used to manage transactions. COMMIT: Permanently saves all changes made during the current transaction. ROLLBACK: Undoes all changes made in the current transaction. SAVEPOINT: Creates a checkpoint within a transaction to rollback to

later. BEGIN; UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE id = 1; SAVEPOINT SP1; UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE id = 2; ROLLBACK TO SP1; -- Undoes the second update COMMIT; -- Permanently saves the first update Join A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column.

Inner Join Returns only rows with matching values in both tables. SELECT A.Name, B.Dept FROM Emp A INNER JOIN Dept B ON A.DeptID = B.DeptID; Outer Joins Left Outer: Returns all rows from the left table, and matched rows from the right. Right Outer: Returns all rows from the right table, and matched rows from the left. Full Outer: Returns all rows when there is a match in either table. Equi join and a natural join, Equi Join Natural Join Explicitly uses the equality operator ( = ) in the ON clause. Implicitly matches on all columns that have the same name . No ON clause is used. Output contains duplicate matching columns. Output automatically removes duplicate matching columns. SELECT * FROM Emp JOIN Dept ON Emp.DeptID = Dept.DeptID; SELECT * FROM Emp NATURAL JOIN Dept; Self join

Self Join A table is joined with itself using aliases. SELECT E.Name AS Employee, M.Name AS Manager FROM Employee E JOIN Employee M ON E.ManagerID = M.EmpID; Cross Join Produces the Cartesian Product of two tables (every row matched with every row). SELECT T.Name, C.RoomNo FROM Teachers T CROSS JOIN Classrooms C; Aggregate functions available in SQL, COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN, giving an example of each Aggregate functions perform a calculation on a set of values and return a single summarizing value. COUNT(): Returns the number of rows. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Employees; SUM(): Returns the total sum of a column. SELECT SUM(Salary) FROM Employees; AVG(): Returns the average value. SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employees; MAX() / MIN(): Returns the largest / smallest value. SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees; Purpose of the GROUP BY clause The GROUP BY clause is used to arrange identical data into groups. It is typically used in conjunction with aggregate functions (COUNT, MAX, MIN, SUM, AVG). Scenario: Find the total number of employees in each department. SELECT DeptID, COUNT(EmpID) AS TotalEmployees FROM Employee GROUP BY DeptID; How is the HAVING clause different from the WHERE clause WHERE Clause HAVING Clause Filters individual rows before grouping. Filters groups after grouping. Cannot contain aggregate functions. Can contain aggregate functions.

Example SELECT DeptID, AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE HireDate > '2020-01-01' -- Filters rows first GROUP BY DeptID HAVING AVG(Salary) > 50000; -- Filters groups Use of the ORDER BY clause The ORDER BY clause is used to sort the result set of a query in either ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order. Example: SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee ORDER BY Salary DESC; Nested queries A nested query (subquery) is a query embedded within another query. They are used to break down complex queries into isolated steps. Scenario: Find employees who earn a salary greater than the average salary. SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee); Correlated subquery Simple Subquery Correlated Subquery Executes completely independent of the outer query. Depends on the outer query for its values. Executes exactly once for the entire outer query. Executes repeatedly , once for every row processed by the outer query.

Example (Correlated) SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee E1 WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee E2 WHERE E1.DeptID = E2.DeptID); Use of IN, EXISTS, ANY and ALL operators in a nested query IN: Checks if a value matches any value in a list or subquery result. WHERE DeptID IN (SELECT DeptID FROM Departments) EXISTS: Evaluates to TRUE if the subquery returns one or more records. WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Orders.CustID = Customers.ID) ANY (or SOME): Compares a value to each value in a list and evaluates to TRUE if any comparison is true. WHERE Salary > ANY (SELECT Salary FROM IT_Dept) ALL: Evaluates to TRUE only if the comparison is true for all values in the list. WHERE Salary > ALL (SELECT Salary FROM Interns) View A View is a virtual table based on the result-set of an SQL statement. It contains rows and columns, just like a real table, but holds no data of its own.

Advantages Security: Restricts access to specific rows/columns of a table. Simplicity: Hides complex joins and calculations into a single virtual table. Data Independence: Insulates applications from changes in base table structures. Simple view and a materialized view Simple View Materialized View Virtual table; does not store data physically. Stores the actual result data physically on disk. Query is executed every time the view is accessed. Data is pre-computed, providing much faster read access. Always shows up-to-date real-time data. Needs to be refreshed periodically to show updated data. Can every view be updated No , not all views can be updated. A view is updatable only if the DBMS can unambiguously trace the update back to the underlying base table rows.

Limitations (Cannot Update If:) It contains aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX). It contains GROUP BY or HAVING clauses. It is built using multiple tables (Joins), depending on the DBMS. It uses the DISTINCT keyword. Example A view CREATE VIEW Dept_Salaries AS SELECT DeptID, AVG(Salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY DeptID; cannot be updated because an update to an average salary cannot be mapped to individual employees. Generalization, specialization and aggregation in the Extended E-R model

Specialization (Top-Down) The process of defining a set of subclasses from an entity type based on distinguishing characteristics. Example: An Employee can be specialized into Hourly_Emp and Salaried_Emp . Generalization (Bottom-Up) The reverse of specialization. Extracting shared characteristics from multiple entity types to create a generalized superclass. Example: Car and Truck generalized into Vehicle . Aggregation Treating a relationship between entities as a single abstract entity, allowing relationships to participate in other relationships. Example: A Project and Employee have a Works_On relationship. A Manager manages the entire Works_On relationship, treating it as one aggregated entity. Decomposition Decomposition is the process of breaking down a large, poorly-designed relation into two or more smaller relations to eliminate redundancy and anomalies.

Lossless-Join Decomposition A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if joining R1 and R2 back together using a Natural Join yields the exact original relation R, without generating spurious (fake) tuples. Condition: The common attributes must be a candidate key for at least one of the decomposed relations (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2 ). Dependency-Preserving Decomposition A decomposition is dependency-preserving if all original functional dependencies can be checked and enforced using only the decomposed relations, without needing to join them back together. How is decomposition related to normalization Normalization uses Decomposition as its primary mechanism. When a relation violates a normal form, we decompose it into smaller relations that satisfy the normal form.

Example Suppose a relation R(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID → EmpName, DeptID and DeptID → DeptName . This violates 3NF due to the transitive dependency ( EmpID → DeptID → DeptName ). Normalization Process: We decompose R into two relations to remove the redundancy: 1. Employee(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID) 2. Department(DeptID, DeptName) This decomposition is both lossless-join (because DeptID is a primary key in Department) and dependency-preserving. Expression: π sid (Enrollment) ÷ π cid (Course) To get the student names, we natural join this result with the Student table: π sname ( Student ⨝ (π sid, cid (Enrollment) ÷ π cid (Course)) ) Write a correlated subquery to list students who have scored more than the average marks obtained in their respective course SELECT s.sname, e1.cid, e1.marks FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e1 ON s.sid = e1.sid WHERE e1.marks > ( SELECT AVG(e2.marks) FROM Enrollment e2 WHERE e1.cid = e2.cid ); The inner query recalculates the average marks dynamically for every row of the outer query, matching the cid .

Unit III: Advanced SQL & Transactions Use of CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE commands CREATE TABLE is used to create a new table in the database. ALTER TABLE is used to add, delete, or modify columns in an existing table. DROP TABLE is used to delete an existing table completely (including its structure and data). DDL statements are auto-committed because they alter the database schema directly and cannot be rolled back in most RDBMS like MySQL and Oracle. Write a CREATE TABLE statement for a Library_Book table having Book_ID, Title, Author, Price and Published_Date, choosing appropriate data types CREATE TABLE Library_Book ( Book_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Title VARCHAR(100), Author VARCHAR(50), Price DECIMAL(8,2), Published_Date DATE ); Write a query to add a column Email of type VARCHAR(40) to the Student table ALTER TABLE Student ADD Email VARCHAR(40); Write a query to change the data type of the Fees column in the Student table to DECIMAL(10,2) ALTER TABLE Student MODIFY Fees DECIMAL(10,2); Write a query to rename the Course column of the Student table as Program ALTER TABLE Student RENAME COLUMN Course TO Program; (Note: Syntax varies slightly between RDBMS. In older MySQL versions, CHANGE Course Program VARCHAR(...) is used).

Write a query to rename the table Student to Student_Info ALTER TABLE Student RENAME TO Student_Info; Alternatively: RENAME TABLE Student TO Student_Info; Using CREATE TABLE CREATE TABLE Student_Backup AS SELECT * FROM Student; Give the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP commands DELETE is a DML command used to remove specific rows based on a WHERE clause. It can be rolled back. TRUNCATE is a DDL command that removes all rows from a table quickly by deallocating the pages. It cannot be rolled back and resets identity columns. DROP is a DDL command that completely deletes the table structure and its data from the database. Five constraints NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK, giving an example of each NOT NULL : Ensures a column cannot have a NULL value. Ex: Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE : Ensures all values in a column are distinct. Ex: Email VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE PRIMARY KEY : Uniquely identifies each record. It is NOT NULL + UNIQUE. Ex: ID INT PRIMARY KEY FOREIGN KEY : Ensures referential integrity by linking to a primary key in another table. Ex: FOREIGN KEY (DeptID) REFERENCES Dept(ID) CHECK : Ensures values in a column satisfy a specific

condition. Ex: Age INT CHECK (Age >= 18) Column-level and a table-level constraint Column-level constraints are defined immediately after the data type of a column. Table-level constraints are defined at the end of the table creation and can span multiple columns. A table-level constraint is compulsory when defining a composite key (a constraint that involves more than one column). Write a CREATE TABLE statement for Department(Dept_ID, Dept_Name), keeping Dept_ID as the primary key CREATE TABLE Department ( Dept_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Dept_Name VARCHAR(50) ); Write a CREATE TABLE statement for Employee(Emp_ID, Name, Email, Dept_ID, Salary), where Emp_ID is the primary key, Name cannot be left blank and Email must be unique CREATE TABLE Employee ( Emp_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Email VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE, Dept_ID INT, Salary DECIMAL(10,2) ); Using ALTER TABLE, add a foreign key on Employee ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT fk_dept FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(Dept_ID); Using ALTER TABLE, put a check constraint on the Employee table so that Salary is always greater than zero ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT chk_salary CHECK (Salary > 0); Table can have more than one UNIQUE constraint but only one PRIMARY KEY A Primary Key is strictly designed to

be the single, definitive row identifier used by the database engine to organize and index the physical storage (e.g. clustered index). There can only be one physical ordering. However, multiple columns may have naturally unique data (like an Email or Phone number), which is why multiple UNIQUE constraints are permitted to enforce business rules. Numeric functions ROUND, TRUNCATE, CEIL, FLOOR, ABS, MOD, POWER and SQRT, giving an example of each ROUND(n, d) : Rounds n to d decimal places. ROUND(3.456, 2) → 3.46 TRUNCATE(n, d) : Cuts off n at d decimal places without rounding. TRUNCATE(3.456, 2) → 3.45 CEIL(n) : Returns the smallest integer ≥ n . CEIL(3.14) → 4 FLOOR(n) : Returns the largest integer ≤ n . FLOOR(3.8) → 3 ABS(n) : Returns the absolute (positive) value. ABS(-5) → 5 MOD(x, y) : Returns the remainder of x/y. MOD(10, 3) → 1 POWER(x, y) : Returns x raised to power y. POWER(2, 3) → 8 SQRT(n) : Returns the square root. SQRT(16) → 4 Round off 78 SELECT ROUND(78.3456, 2); -- Result: 78.35 SELECT TRUNCATE(78.3456, 2); -- Result: 78.34 Reason : ROUND evaluates the third decimal digit (5) and mathematically rounds up. TRUNCATE simply drops all digits

after the 2nd decimal place without any mathematical evaluation. Write a query on PRODUCT_MAST to display each Product_Name along SELECT Product_Name, ROUND(Price, 0) AS Rounded_Price FROM PRODUCT_MAST; Find the remainder when 29 is divided by 4 -- Find remainder SELECT MOD(29, 4); -- Check if odd/even (if remainder is 1, it is odd) SELECT MOD(29, 2); Find the square of 12 SELECT POWER(12, 2) AS Square, SQRT(144) AS Root; Date functions CURDATE, DATEDIFF, DATE_ADD/DATE_SUB and DATE_FORMAT, giving an example of each CURDATE() : Returns the current system date. Ex: SELECT CURDATE(); DATEDIFF(date1, date2) : Returns the number of days between two dates. Ex: SELECT DATEDIFF('2023-10-10', '2023-10-01'); → 9 DATE_ADD(date, INTERVAL expr unit) : Adds a time interval to a date. Ex: SELECT DATE_ADD('2023-01-01', INTERVAL 5 DAY); DATE_FORMAT(date, format) : Formats a date string. Ex: SELECT DATE_FORMAT(CURDATE(), '%Y-%m-%d'); String functions CONCAT, UPPER/LOWER, LENGTH, SUBSTRING and TRIM/REPLACE, giving an example of each CONCAT(s1, s2) : Joins two or more strings. Ex: CONCAT('Data', 'base') → 'Database' UPPER(s) / LOWER(s) : Converts a string to all uppercase or lowercase. Ex: UPPER('sql') → 'SQL' LENGTH(s) : Returns the number of characters in a string. Ex: LENGTH('DBMS') → 4 SUBSTRING(s, start, len) : Extracts a part

of a string. Ex: SUBSTRING('Database', 1, 4) → 'Data' TRIM(s) : Removes leading and trailing spaces. Ex: TRIM(' SQL ') → 'SQL' REPLACE(s, old, new) : Replaces all occurrences of a substring. Ex: REPLACE('DBMS', 'M', 'B') → 'DBBS' Using DATEDIFF, find the number of days between '2023-01-01' and '2023-12-31' SELECT DATEDIFF('2023-12-31', '2023-01-01') AS Days_Difference; (Note: Syntax may vary slightly by DBMS. In MySQL, it returns 364.) Using DATE_ADD, add 45 days to the date '2024-02-01' SELECT DATE_ADD('2024-02-01', INTERVAL 45 DAY) AS New_Date; Write a query to extract only the year and month from the date '2025-03-22' SELECT YEAR('2025-03-22') AS Year, MONTH('2025-03-22') AS Month; Alternatively, using DATE_FORMAT in MySQL: SELECT DATE_FORMAT('2025-03-22', '%Y-%m'); Write a query on the STUDENT table that displays the full name of every student by joining First_Name and Last_Name SELECT CONCAT(First_Name, ' ', Last_Name) AS Full_Name FROM STUDENT; Find the length of the string 'Normalization', and separately extract its first six characters SELECT LENGTH('Normalization') AS Str_Length, SUBSTRING('Normalization', 1, 6) AS Extracted_Str; UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT and MINUS/EXCEPT Set Operators: UNION : Combines results of two queries, removing duplicates. UNION ALL : Combines results of two queries, keeping all duplicates. INTERSECT : Returns only the rows that appear in

both queries. MINUS / EXCEPT : Returns rows from the first query that are not present in the second. Condition for application (Union Compatibility): Both SELECT statements must have the same number of columns. The corresponding columns must have compatible data types in the same order. Write a query to list every student who is a member of CLUB_CODING or CLUB_MUSIC or both, SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING UNION SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC; Write a query that lists all the rows of CLUB_CODING and CLUB_MUSIC together without removing duplicate names SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING UNION ALL SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC; Write a query to find students who are members of both CLUB_CODING and CLUB_MUSIC SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING INTERSECT SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC; Write a query to find students who are in CLUB_CODING but not in CLUB_MUSIC SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING EXCEPT -- (or MINUS in Oracle) SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC; Yes, the order matters. A EXCEPT B returns elements in A that are not in B. B EXCEPT A would return students in CLUB_MUSIC who are not in CLUB_CODING. Transaction A transaction is a logical unit of work consisting of one or more SQL statements that must be executed entirely

or not at all. ACID Properties (Bank Transfer Example: A to B): Atomicity : "All or nothing." If money is deducted from A, it MUST be credited to B. If either fails, the entire transaction is rolled back. Consistency : The database must remain in a valid state. The total sum of A + B's balances must be the same before and after the transaction. Isolation : Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. If another transaction reads A's balance during the transfer, it will see the state either strictly before or strictly after, not midway. Durability : Once the transaction is committed, the changes are permanent and will survive system crashes. Transaction State Diagram COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT COMMIT : Saves all changes made during the current transaction permanently. ROLLBACK : Undoes all changes made during the current transaction, reverting to the last commit. SAVEPOINT : Sets a marker within a transaction so you can roll back to that specific point without canceling the entire transaction. START TRANSACTION; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A101'; SAVEPOINT step1; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; -- If something goes

wrong here: ROLLBACK TO step1; -- Undoes only the A102 update COMMIT; -- Saves the final state Write a transaction that transfers Rs START TRANSACTION; SAVEPOINT before_transfer; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A103'; COMMIT; Using a searched CASE statement, classify each account's Balance as 'High' if it is 25000 or more, 'Medium' if it is 15000 or more, and 'Low' otherwise SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance, CASE WHEN Balance >= 25000 THEN 'High' WHEN Balance >= 15000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Low' END AS Balance_Category FROM ACCOUNT; Write a query SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance, IF(Balance < 15000, 'Low Balance Alert', 'OK') AS Status FROM ACCOUNT; Write a query SELECT Acc_No, Name, COALESCE(Nominee_Name, 'Not Registered') AS Nominee FROM ACCOUNT; In one or two lines each, state the purpose of a stored procedure, a sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL), a cursor and a trigger Stored Procedure : A pre-compiled collection of SQL statements saved in the database that can be executed as a single callable routine. Sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT) : Automatically generates unique, sequential numeric values, typically used for primary keys. Cursor : A database object used to

retrieve and process rows one by one from a result set inside a stored procedure. Trigger : A special type of stored procedure that automatically executes (fires) in response to specific DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a table. BEFORE trigger and an AFTER trigger BEFORE Trigger executes before the triggering DML operation is applied (useful for validation/modification of incoming data). AFTER Trigger executes after the operation (useful for auditing or cascading changes to other tables). NEW refers to the incoming data (being inserted or updated). OLD refers to the existing data in the table before the operation (being updated or deleted). Purpose of exception handling in a stored procedure Exception handling ensures that if an error occurs during execution, the stored procedure can catch it and gracefully handle it (e.g., rolling back a transaction) instead of crashing. DECLARE ... HANDLER : Defines a block of code to execute when a specific error or condition occurs (e.g., DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION ). SIGNAL : Used to artificially raise a custom error or exception, returning a custom SQLSTATE and message to the caller.

title: Define programming paradigm and name any two programming paradigms other than OOP.
chunks: A programming paradigm is a fundamental style or approach to programming, dictating how tasks are structured and executed. Two other paradigms besides Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) are: Procedural Programming (e.g., C) Functional Programming (e.g., Haskell, LISP)
subject: java

title: When was Java officially announced by Sun Microsystems, and what was its original name?
chunks: Java was officially announced by Sun Microsystems in 1995 . Its original name during development was Oak (named after an oak tree outside James Gosling's office).
subject: java

title: Define Object-Oriented Programming and list the six pillars of OOP.
chunks: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a paradigm centered around "objects" (which contain data in the form of fields and code in the form of methods) rather than "actions" or logic. The six pillars (or core concepts) of OOP are: Class Object Encapsulation Abstraction Inheritance Polymorphism
subject: java

title: Differentiate between a class and an object with one suitable example.
chunks: Class Object A logical template or blueprint. A physical entity/instance created from a class. Does not allocate memory when created. Allocates memory in the heap when instantiated. Declared using the class keyword. Created using the new keyword. Example: If Car is a class (the blueprint), then a Red Tesla Model S is an object (an actual car).
subject: java

title: Define encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism.
chunks: Encapsulation: Wrapping data (variables) and code (methods) together into a single unit (class), protecting the data from outside interference. Abstraction: Hiding internal implementation details and exposing only the necessary functionalities to the user. Inheritance: A mechanism where a new class (child) inherits properties and behaviors from an existing class (parent), promoting code reusability. Polymorphism: The ability of a single entity (method, object, or operator) to take on multiple forms and behave differently based on the context.
subject: java

title: What is the difference between procedural and object-oriented programming?
chunks: Procedural Programming (POP) Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Program is divided into small parts called functions . Program is divided into parts called objects . Follows a Top-Down approach. Follows a Bottom-Up approach. Data is freely moving and less secure. Data is hidden (encapsulated) and highly secure. Example: C, Pascal Example: Java, C++, Python
subject: java

title: What are JDK, JRE, and JVM?
chunks: JDK (Java Development Kit): A full software development environment. It contains the JRE plus development tools like the compiler ( javac ) and debugger. JRE (Java Runtime Environment): The environment required to run Java programs. It contains the JVM and core class libraries. JVM (Java Virtual Machine): An abstract machine that executes Java Bytecode. It makes Java platform-independent.
subject: java

title: What is bytecode, and why is Java considered platform-independent?
chunks: Bytecode is a highly optimized set of instructions generated by the Java compiler ( javac ) after compiling the source code. It is not machine code, but rather intermediate code. Java is platform-independent because the compiler generates this bytecode instead of native machine code. This bytecode can be executed on any operating system as long as that system has a JVM (Java Virtual Machine) installed to interpret it (Write Once, Run Anywhere).
subject: java

title: What is a Java package? Give two examples of commonly used packages.
chunks: A Java package is a mechanism for organizing related classes and interfaces into a single namespace. It prevents naming conflicts and controls access (encapsulation). Two Examples: java.util (Contains utility classes like Scanner, ArrayList) java.lang (Contains core classes like String, Math. It is imported automatically)
subject: java

title: List the four access modifiers in Java and state the default access level.
chunks: The four access modifiers in Java (from most restrictive to least) are: private (accessible only within the same class) default (no keyword; accessible only within the same package) protected (accessible within the same package and subclasses in other packages) public (accessible from anywhere) If no modifier is specified, the access level is default (package-private).
subject: java

title: What is a class and what is an object in Java? Give one difference between them.
chunks: A class is a user-defined blueprint or prototype from which objects are created. An object is a runtime instance of a class that has state and behavior. Difference: A class is a logical entity that consumes no memory upon declaration, whereas an object is a physical entity that consumes memory space in the heap when instantiated.
subject: java

title: What is the purpose of the new keyword in Java? Where is the newly created object stored?
chunks: The new keyword in Java is used to create a new object or array by allocating memory at runtime. It essentially instantiates a class. Storage: The newly created object is always stored in the Heap memory.
subject: java

title: What is the difference between an instance variable and a local variable? State any two differences.
chunks: Instance Variable Local Variable Declared inside a class but outside any method. Declared inside a method, constructor, or block. Gets a default value (e.g., 0 for int) if not initialized. Does not get a default value; must be initialized before use.
subject: java

title: What is a constructor in Java? State any two rules of a constructor.
chunks: A constructor is a special block of code that is called automatically when an object is instantiated. It is used to initialize the state of the object. Rules: The constructor name must exactly match the class name. A constructor must not have an explicit return type (not even void ).
subject: java

title: What is constructor overloading? On what basis does the compiler distinguish overloaded constructors?
chunks: Constructor Overloading is a technique of having more than one constructor in a class with different parameter lists. It allows objects to be initialized in different ways. The compiler distinguishes them based on the number of parameters , the types of the parameters , and the order of the parameters .
subject: java

title: What is constructor chaining? Name the two keywords used for constructor chaining.
chunks: Constructor chaining is the process of calling one constructor from another constructor with respect to the current object. It helps avoid duplicate code. The two keywords used are: this() : Used to call a constructor of the same class. super() : Used to call a constructor of the superclass (parent class).
subject: java

title: What is the purpose of the this keyword in Java? State any two uses.
chunks: The this keyword is a reference variable that refers to the current object on which the method or constructor is being invoked. Two Uses: To resolve shadowing when instance variables and local parameters share the same name (e.g., this.name = name; ). To invoke another constructor in the same class (using this() ).
subject: java

title: What is Garbage Collection in Java? When does an object become eligible for garbage collection?
chunks: Garbage Collection (GC) is the process by which Java programs perform automatic memory management, freeing up the heap by deleting objects that are no longer in use. An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when it is completely unreferenced (i.e., no live thread can access it). This happens if its reference is set to null , if it is created anonymously, or if references are reassigned.
subject: java

title: What is autoboxing and unboxing in Java?
chunks: Autoboxing: The automatic conversion that the Java compiler makes between the primitive types and their corresponding object wrapper classes (e.g., converting int to Integer ). Unboxing: The reverse process; converting an object of a wrapper type back to its corresponding primitive value (e.g., converting Integer to int ).
subject: java

title: What is String immutability? State one benefit of immutable Strings.
chunks: String immutability means that once a String object is created, its value or state cannot be changed. Any operation that alters the string creates a brand new String object rather than modifying the original. Benefit: It makes Strings thread-safe and allows caching in the String Constant Pool, which saves memory.
subject: java

title: Define inheritance. List the different types of inheritance supported in Java.
chunks: Inheritance is a mechanism where a new class acquires the properties and methods of an existing class, establishing an IS-A relationship and promoting code reuse. Types supported in Java (via classes): Single Inheritance Multilevel Inheritance Hierarchical Inheritance (Note: Multiple and Hybrid inheritance are not supported through classes, only through interfaces).
subject: java

title: What is the purpose of the super keyword? List any two uses.
chunks: The super keyword is a reference variable used to refer to the immediate parent class object. Two Uses: To invoke the immediate parent class constructor (e.g., super(); ). To invoke an overridden method in the parent class (e.g., super.display(); ).
subject: java

title: What is the Object class? Name any two methods of the Object class.
chunks: The Object class (located in the java.lang package) is the root class of the Java class hierarchy. Every class in Java directly or indirectly inherits from the Object class. Two Methods: toString() equals(Object obj)
subject: java

title: Define method overloading and method overriding.
chunks: Method Overloading: Creating multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameters (compile-time polymorphism). Method Overriding: Providing a specific implementation in a subclass for a method that is already defined in its parent class. The method signature must be identical (run-time polymorphism).
subject: java

title: What is polymorphism? Name its two types.
chunks: Polymorphism is the ability of an object or method to take on many forms, allowing the same interface to be used for different underlying forms (data types). Two Types: Compile-time Polymorphism (Static binding, e.g., Method Overloading). Run-time Polymorphism (Dynamic binding, e.g., Method Overriding).
subject: java

title: What is dynamic binding? Why is it also called late binding?
chunks: Dynamic Binding is the process where the compiler does not resolve the method call at compile time, but rather the JVM determines the actual method implementation to execute at runtime based on the actual object type. It is called late binding because the binding of the method call to the method body is delayed until the program is actually executing.
subject: java

title: Define upcasting and downcasting in Java.
chunks: Upcasting: Casting a subclass reference variable to a superclass reference. This is done automatically and implicitly by the compiler. Downcasting: Casting a superclass reference variable back to a subclass reference. This must be done explicitly by the programmer and requires checking to prevent ClassCastException .
subject: java

title: What is the purpose of the instanceof operator?
chunks: The instanceof operator is a binary operator used to test whether a given object is an instance of a specific class, subclass, or interface. It returns true or false . It is primarily used to check object types before attempting a downcast , preventing runtime exceptions.
subject: java

title: What is an abstract class? What is an interface?
chunks: Abstract Class: A class declared with the abstract keyword that cannot be instantiated. It can contain both abstract methods (without a body) and concrete methods. Interface: A completely "abstract class" that acts as a contract. In modern Java, it primarily contains abstract methods and static constants, though it can now have default methods. A class implements an interface.
subject: java

title: What are generics in Java? Give one example of a generic type parameter.
chunks: Generics enable types (classes and interfaces) to be parameters when defining classes, interfaces and methods. This provides stronger type checks at compile time and removes the need for explicit casting. Example: <T> is a generic type parameter where T stands for Type. Example usage: List<String> list = new ArrayList<String>();
subject: java

title: Explain the Top-Down and Bottom-Up approaches with a suitable example.
chunks: Top-Down Approach: The problem is broken down into smaller sub-problems. It focuses on the main algorithm first, then the details (used in Procedural Programming like C). Example: Building a car by first designing the full car, then breaking it down into engine, wheels, and doors. Bottom-Up Approach: The smaller modules or objects are designed first, and then integrated together to form the complete system (used in Object-Oriented Programming like Java). Example: Designing the engine, wheels, and doors first as independent objects, then assembling them to build the car.
subject: java

title: Explain how Java evolved from Oak and mention any three important features of Java.
chunks: Java was originally developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems in 1991 for interactive television and consumer electronics. It was initially named Oak . It was later renamed Java in 1995 and shifted focus to the World Wide Web because of its platform independence. Three Important Features: Platform Independent: Write once, run anywhere (WORA) using Bytecode and JVM. Object-Oriented: Everything is an object; follows OOP principles strictly. Robust & Secure: Strong memory management, automatic garbage collection, and no explicit pointers.
subject: java

title: Explain the role of JDK, JRE, and JVM in executing a Java program.
chunks: JDK (Java Development Kit): The complete toolbox for a developer. It provides the compiler ( javac ) which translates the .java source code into a .class file (bytecode). JRE (Java Runtime Environment): The environment where the Java program runs. It provides the core class libraries and packages required for execution. JVM (Java Virtual Machine): The core engine inside the JRE. It reads the bytecode line by line, interprets it, and executes it on the host operating system.
subject: java

title: Explain the basic structure of a Java program and write the standard main() method signature.
chunks: A basic Java program consists of a class definition containing methods. The entry point of any standalone Java application is the main method. public class HelloWorld { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Hello, World!"); } } public : Accessible from anywhere. static : Can be called without instantiating the class. void : Returns nothing. String[] args : Command-line arguments.
subject: java

title: Explain Java identifiers, naming rules, comments, and the importance of proper coding conventions.
chunks: Identifiers: Names given to classes, variables, and methods. Rules: Must start with a letter, _ , or $ . Cannot be a keyword. Case-sensitive. Comments: Used to explain code. Single-line ( // ) and Multi-line ( /* ... */ ). Coding Conventions: Classes: PascalCase Methods/Variables: camelCase Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE Importance: Improves code readability, maintainability, and collaboration among developers.
subject: java

title: Explain built-in and user-defined packages with suitable examples. Also explain the purpose of the import statement.
chunks: Built-in Packages: Provided by the Java API. Example: java.util , java.io . User-defined Packages: Created by the programmer to group related classes. Example: package com.mycompany.utils; Import Statement: Used to bring a class or an entire package into visibility so it can be used without typing its fully qualified name (e.g., import java.util.Scanner; ).

title: Explain the four access modifiers in Java with respect to their accessibility.
chunks: Modifier Same Class Same Package Subclass (Diff Pkg) Diff Pkg (Non-subclass) Private Yes No No No Default Yes Yes No No Protected Yes Yes Yes No Public Yes Yes Yes Yes

title: Differentiate between variable scope and lifetime. Also explain dynamic initialization.
chunks: Scope: The region of the code where a variable is visible and accessible (e.g., block scope, method scope). Lifetime: The duration of time a variable exists in memory during program execution. Dynamic Initialization: Initializing a variable at runtime using an expression or method call, rather than a hardcoded constant. Example: double c = Math.sqrt(a*a + b*b);
subject: java

title: Explain Java data types and differentiate between primitive and reference data types.
chunks: Primitive Data Types: Predefined by Java and hold actual values. There are 8: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean . They are stored in stack memory and have a fixed size. Reference Data Types: User-defined (except Arrays and Strings) and hold references (memory addresses) to the actual objects. They are stored in heap memory. Examples: Classes, Interfaces, Arrays.

title: Explain one-dimensional and two-dimensional arrays, and differentiate between for, while, and do-while loops.

title: Explain the difference between stack and heap memory in Java with respect to object creation and references.

Stack Memory: This is where all local variables, method calls, and object references are stored. When you write Car c = new Car(); , the object itself goes in the heap, but the reference variable c is kept in the stack, pointing to the heap memory address.

title: Explain the two ways of creating a String in Java: using a string literal and using the new keyword.

title: Differentiate between compile-time and run-time polymorphism in Java.
chunks: Compile-time Polymorphism: Achieved through Method Overloading. The compiler knows exactly which method to call based on the method signature (number and type of arguments). Fast execution because binding happens early. Run-time Polymorphism: Achieved through Method Overriding. A parent reference points to a child object. The JVM determines which overridden method to execute during runtime based on the actual object type , not the reference type.

title: Explain dynamic binding and object casting with reference to upcasting and downcasting.
chunks: Dynamic Binding is resolving a method call at runtime depending on the actual object. Upcasting: Casting a subclass to a superclass. It is automatic. Animal a = new Dog(); This triggers dynamic binding when overridden methods are called. Downcasting: Casting a superclass back to a subclass. It must be explicit. Dog d = (Dog) a; This is needed to access methods specific only to the child class.

title: Explain the instanceof operator and its importance before performing downcasting.
chunks: The instanceof operator checks if an object is an instance of a specific class or interface. Importance in Downcasting: Downcasting a parent reference to a child reference is dangerous because if the parent reference doesn't actually hold that specific child object, the JVM throws a ClassCastException . Using if (obj instanceof Dog) { Dog d = (Dog) obj; } ensures the downcast is mathematically safe.

Only public static final constants. A class can extend only one abstract class. A class can implement multiple interfaces. Multiple Inheritance: Java prevents a class from extending multiple classes to avoid ambiguity, but it allows a class to implement multiple interfaces because interfaces (traditionally) have no implementation to clash.

title: Explain the six pillars of OOP—class, object, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism—with suitable examples.
chunks: Class: A blueprint for creating objects. Ex: A Vehicle class defining speed and color. Object: A real-world instance of a class. Ex: A specific red Ferrari. Encapsulation: Wrapping data and methods into a single unit to protect the data. Ex: A capsule containing medicine; private variables accessed via getters/setters. Abstraction: Hiding complex implementation details and showing only essentials. Ex: Driving a car without knowing how the internal combustion engine works. Inheritance: A child class acquiring properties from a parent class. Ex: Dog inherits from Animal . Polymorphism: One entity taking many forms. Ex: A sound() method that barks for a Dog but meows for a Cat.

title: Explain Java's platform independence in detail, from source code compilation to bytecode execution through the JVM.
chunks: Java's "Write Once, Run Anywhere" capability relies on its two-step execution process: Compilation: The developer writes Program.java (Source Code). The Java Compiler ( javac ) compiles this into Program.class . Instead of compiling it into machine-specific code (like C++), it compiles it into Bytecode . This bytecode is entirely independent of the underlying OS or hardware. Execution: The compiled bytecode is transported to any machine (Windows, Mac, Linux). That machine must have a JVM (Java Virtual Machine) installed. The JVM reads the bytecode and translates it into the specific machine-level instructions native to that exact operating system. Therefore, while the JVM is platform- dependent , the Java program (bytecode) itself is totally platform- independent .
