Unit I: Java Basics Programming paradigm and name any two programming paradigms other than OOP A programming paradigm is a fundamental style or approach to programming, dictating how tasks are structured and executed. Two other paradigms besides Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) are: Procedural Programming (e.g., C) Functional Programming (e.g., Haskell, LISP) When was Java officially announced by Sun Microsystems, and what was its original name Java was officially announced by Sun Microsystems in 1995 . Its original name during development was Oak (named after an oak tree outside James Gosling's office). Procedural and object-oriented programming Procedural Programming (POP) Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Program is divided into small parts called functions . Program is divided into parts called objects . Follows a Top-Down approach. Follows a Bottom-Up approach. Data is freely moving and less secure. Data is hidden (encapsulated) and highly secure. Example: C, Pascal Example: Java, C++, Python JDK, JRE, and JVM JDK (Java Development Kit): A full software development environment. It contains the JRE plus development tools like the compiler ( javac ) and debugger. JRE (Java Runtime Environment): The environment required to run Java programs. It contains the JVM and core class libraries. JVM (Java Virtual Machine): An abstract machine

that executes Java Bytecode. It makes Java platform-independent. Bytecode, and why is Java considered platform-independent Bytecode is a highly optimized set of instructions generated by the Java compiler ( javac ) after compiling the source code. It is not machine code, but rather intermediate code. Java is platform-independent because the compiler generates this bytecode instead of native machine code. This bytecode can be executed on any operating system as long as that system has a JVM (Java Virtual Machine) installed to interpret it (Write Once, Run Anywhere). Instance variable and a local variable Instance Variable Local Variable Declared inside a class but outside any method. Declared inside a method, constructor, or block. Gets a default value (e.g., 0 for int) if not initialized. Does not get a default value; must be initialized before use. Method overloading and method overriding Method Overloading: Creating multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameters (compile-time polymorphism). Method Overriding: Providing a specific implementation in a subclass for a method that is already defined in its parent class. The method signature must be identical (run-time polymorphism). Top-Down and Bottom-Up approaches Top-Down Approach: The problem is broken down into smaller sub-problems. It

focuses on the main algorithm first, then the details (used in Procedural Programming like C). Example: Building a car by first designing the full car, then breaking it down into engine, wheels, and doors. Bottom-Up Approach: The smaller modules or objects are designed first, and then integrated together to form the complete system (used in Object-Oriented Programming like Java). Example: Designing the engine, wheels, and doors first as independent objects, then assembling them to build the car. Java evolved from Oak and mention any three important features of Java Java was originally developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems in 1991 for interactive television and consumer electronics. It was initially named Oak . It was later renamed Java in 1995 and shifted focus to the World Wide Web because of its platform independence. Three Important Features: Platform Independent: Write once, run anywhere (WORA) using Bytecode and JVM. Object-Oriented: Everything is an object; follows OOP principles strictly. Robust & Secure: Strong memory management, automatic garbage collection, and no explicit pointers. Role of JDK, JRE, and JVM in executing a Java program JDK (Java Development Kit): The complete toolbox for a developer. It provides the compiler ( javac ) which translates the

.java source code into a .class file (bytecode). JRE (Java Runtime Environment): The environment where the Java program runs. It provides the core class libraries and packages required for execution. JVM (Java Virtual Machine): The core engine inside the JRE. It reads the bytecode line by line, interprets it, and executes it on the host operating system. Basic structure of a Java program and write the standard main() method signature A basic Java program consists of a class definition containing methods. The entry point of any standalone Java application is the main method. public class HelloWorld { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Hello, World!"); } } public : Accessible from anywhere. static : Can be called without instantiating the class. void : Returns nothing. String[] args : Command-line arguments. Java identifiers, naming rules, comments, and the importance of proper coding conventions Identifiers: Names given to classes, variables, and methods. Rules: Must start with a letter, _ , or $ . Cannot be a keyword. Case-sensitive. Comments: Used to explain code. Single-line ( // ) and Multi-line ( /* ... */ ). Coding Conventions: Classes: PascalCase Methods/Variables: camelCase Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE Importance: Improves code readability, maintainability, and collaboration among developers. Variable

scope and lifetime Scope: The region of the code where a variable is visible and accessible (e.g., block scope, method scope). Lifetime: The duration of time a variable exists in memory during program execution. Dynamic Initialization: Initializing a variable at runtime using an expression or method call, rather than a hardcoded constant. Example: double c = Math.sqrt(a*a + b*b); Java data types and differentiate between primitive and reference data types Primitive Data Types: Predefined by Java and hold actual values. There are 8: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean . They are stored in stack memory and have a fixed size. Reference Data Types: User-defined (except Arrays and Strings) and hold references (memory addresses) to the actual objects. They are stored in heap memory. Examples: Classes, Interfaces, Arrays. One-dimensional and two-dimensional arrays, and differentiate between for, while, and do-while loops Arrays: 1D Array: A linear list of elements. int[] arr = new int[5]; 2D Array: An array of arrays (a matrix). int[][] matrix = new int[3][3]; Loops: for: Used when the number of iterations is known in advance. while: Used when iterations are unknown; condition is checked before execution (entry-controlled). do-while: Condition is checked after execution (exit-controlled); guarantees

execution at least once. Procedural programming and OOP Feature Procedural Programming Object-Oriented Programming Approach Top-Down approach. Bottom-Up approach. Data Handling Data moves freely between functions globally. Data is tied to objects and controlled via methods. Security Low security (no access modifiers). High security (data hiding via encapsulation & modifiers). Reusability Low (code duplication is common). High (achieved via Inheritance and objects). Inheritance Not supported. Supported (Single, Multilevel, Hierarchical). Polymorphism Not supported. Supported (Overloading, Overriding). Java's platform independence in detail, from source code compilation to bytecode execution through the JVM Java's "Write Once, Run Anywhere" capability relies on its two-step execution process: Compilation: The developer writes Program.java (Source Code). The Java Compiler ( javac ) compiles this into Program.class . Instead of compiling it into machine-specific code (like C++), it compiles it into Bytecode . This bytecode is entirely independent of the underlying OS or hardware. Execution: The compiled bytecode is transported to any machine (Windows, Mac, Linux). That machine must have a JVM (Java Virtual Machine) installed. The JVM reads the bytecode and translates it into the specific machine-level instructions native to that exact operating system. Therefore, while the JVM is platform- dependent , the Java program (bytecode) itself is

totally platform- independent . Java data types, arrays, and operators Data Types: Primitives ( int x = 5; ) and References ( String s = "Hi"; ). Arrays: Homogeneous collections. int[] arr = {1, 2, 3}; Operators: Arithmetic ( + , - ), Relational ( > , == ), Logical ( && , || ). Evaluation of 5 + 3 * 2 % 4 : Precedence of * and % is higher than + . They evaluate left-to-right. 3 * 2 = 6 6 % 4 = 2 (Remainder of 6 divided by 4) 5 + 2 = 7 Write a Java program public class AverageMarks { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] marks = {85, 90, 78, 92, 88}; int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < marks.length; i++) { sum += marks[i]; } double average = (double) sum / marks.length; System.out.println("Average Marks: " + average); } } Java control statements if-else: Branching based on a boolean. if(x > 0) { ... } else { ... } switch-case: Multi-way branch. switch(day) { case 1: ... break; } loops: Repeating code. for(int i=0; i<5; i++) { ... } break: Exits the entire loop or switch immediately.

continue: Skips the current iteration and proceeds to the next iteration of the loop. Ternary Operator: A one-line if-else. int max = (a > b) ? a : b; Write a Java program that uses an array, loop, and conditional statement to count negative numbers and display the result public class NegativeCounter { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] numbers = {5, -2, 9, -8, 0, -1, 3}; int count = 0; for(int num : numbers) { if(num < 0) { count++; } } System.out.println("Total negative numbers: " + count); } }

Unit II: OOP Concepts Object-Oriented Programming and list the six pillars of OOP Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a paradigm centered around "objects" (which contain data in the form of fields and code in the form of methods) rather than "actions" or logic. The six pillars (or core concepts) of OOP are: Class Object Encapsulation Abstraction Inheritance Polymorphism Class and an object Class Object A logical template or blueprint. A physical entity/instance created from a class. Does not allocate memory when created. Allocates memory in the heap when instantiated. Declared using the class keyword. Created using the new keyword. Example: If Car is a class (the blueprint), then a Red Tesla Model S is an object (an actual car). Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism Encapsulation: Wrapping data (variables) and code (methods) together into a single unit (class), protecting the data from outside interference. Abstraction: Hiding internal implementation details and exposing only the necessary functionalities to the user. Inheritance: A mechanism where a new class (child) inherits properties and behaviors from an existing class (parent), promoting code reusability. Polymorphism: The ability of a single entity (method, object, or operator) to take on multiple forms and behave differently based on the context. List

the four access modifiers in Java and state the default access level The four access modifiers in Java (from most restrictive to least) are: private (accessible only within the same class) default (no keyword; accessible only within the same package) protected (accessible within the same package and subclasses in other packages) public (accessible from anywhere) If no modifier is specified, the access level is default (package-private). Class and what is an object in Java A class is a user-defined blueprint or prototype from which objects are created. An object is a runtime instance of a class that has state and behavior. Difference: A class is a logical entity that consumes no memory upon declaration, whereas an object is a physical entity that consumes memory space in the heap when instantiated. Purpose of the new keyword in Java The new keyword in Java is used to create a new object or array by allocating memory at runtime. It essentially instantiates a class. Storage: The newly created object is always stored in the Heap memory. Constructor in Java A constructor is a special block of code that is called automatically when an object is instantiated. It is used to initialize the state

of the object. Rules: The constructor name must exactly match the class name. A constructor must not have an explicit return type (not even void ). Constructor overloading Constructor Overloading is a technique of having more than one constructor in a class with different parameter lists. It allows objects to be initialized in different ways. The compiler distinguishes them based on the number of parameters , the types of the parameters , and the order of the parameters . Constructor chaining Constructor chaining is the process of calling one constructor from another constructor with respect to the current object. It helps avoid duplicate code. The two keywords used are: this() : Used to call a constructor of the same class. super() : Used to call a constructor of the superclass (parent class). Purpose of the this keyword in Java The this keyword is a reference variable that refers to the current object on which the method or constructor is being invoked. Two Uses: To resolve shadowing when instance variables and local parameters share the same name (e.g., this.name = name; ). To invoke another constructor in the same class (using this() ). Autoboxing and unboxing in Java Autoboxing: The automatic

conversion that the Java compiler makes between the primitive types and their corresponding object wrapper classes (e.g., converting int to Integer ). Unboxing: The reverse process; converting an object of a wrapper type back to its corresponding primitive value (e.g., converting Integer to int ). String immutability String immutability means that once a String object is created, its value or state cannot be changed. Any operation that alters the string creates a brand new String object rather than modifying the original. Benefit: It makes Strings thread-safe and allows caching in the String Constant Pool, which saves memory. Four access modifiers in Java Modifier Same Class Same Package Subclass (Diff Pkg) Diff Pkg (Non-subclass) Private Yes No No No Default Yes Yes No No Protected Yes Yes Yes No Public Yes Yes Yes Yes Difference between stack and heap memory in Java Heap Memory: This is where all actual objects and instance variables are stored. It is dynamically allocated at runtime when the new keyword is used. It is managed by the Garbage Collector. Stack Memory: This is where all local variables, method calls, and object references are stored. When you write Car c = new Car(); , the object itself

goes in the heap, but the reference variable c is kept in the stack, pointing to the heap memory address. Default values of instance variables for int, double, char, boolean, and object reference types When instance variables are not explicitly initialized, Java assigns them default values: int (and byte, short, long): 0 double (and float): 0.0 char : '\u0000' (null character) boolean : false Object References (String, arrays, custom classes): null Default/no-argument and parameterized constructors Default / No-Argument Constructor: Takes no parameters. If no constructor is defined, the compiler provides one automatically. Used for default initialization. class Box { Box() { System.out.println("Empty box created"); } } Parameterized Constructor: Takes parameters to initialize the object with specific values upon creation. class Box { int size; Box(int s) { this.size = s; } } Constructor overloading Constructor Overloading allows a class to have multiple constructors with different parameter lists, giving flexibility in how an object is initialized. class Rectangle { int length, width; // Constructor 1: Default (Square) Rectangle() { length = 5; width = 5; } // Constructor 2: Parameterized Rectangle(int l, int w) { length = l; width = w; } } Constructor overloading and constructor chaining Constructor Overloading: Having

multiple separate constructors in the same class to handle different initialization scenarios. Constructor Chaining: The process where one constructor explicitly calls another constructor (either within the same class or from the parent class) to reuse initialization logic. Keywords for Chaining: this() - Calls another constructor in the same class. super() - Calls a constructor in the parent class. Any three uses of the this keyword Resolve Shadowing: Used to distinguish instance variables from local parameters. this.name = name; Constructor Chaining: Used to invoke another constructor in the same class. this(10); // Calls parameterized constructor Pass as Argument: Used to pass the current object as a parameter to another method. helper.printDetails(this); Private, default, protected, and public access modifiers in Java Private: The most restrictive. Accessible only within the class where it is declared. Used for data hiding. Default: (No keyword). Accessible only by classes within the same package. Protected: Accessible within the same package, and by subclasses located in other packages. Public: The least restrictive. Accessible from any class anywhere in the program. Character wrapper class and any four useful methods of the Character class The Character class (in java.lang ) wraps a primitive char value in an object. It provides

numerous utility methods for character manipulation. Four Useful Methods: Character.isLetter(ch) : Returns true if the character is a letter. Character.isDigit(ch) : Returns true if the character is a number. Character.isUpperCase(ch) : Returns true if the character is uppercase. Character.toLowerCase(ch) : Converts the character to lowercase. Two ways of creating a String in Java: String Literal: String s = "Hello"; The JVM first checks the String Constant Pool . If "Hello" exists, it returns the reference. If not, it creates it. This is highly memory-efficient. new Keyword: String s = new String("Hello"); The JVM forces the creation of a brand new String object in the Heap memory, bypassing the pool entirely, even if "Hello" already exists in the pool. = = and equals() when comparing String objects == Operator: Compares the memory references (addresses) of two objects to see if they point to the exact same object in memory. equals() Method: Compares the actual contents/values of the two objects for logical equality. String s1 = new String("Java"); String s2 = new String("Java"); System.out.println(s1 == s2); // false (different heap objects) System.out.println(s1.equals(s2)); // true (same content) Six pillars of OOP—class, object, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism—with suitable examples Class: A blueprint for

creating objects. Ex: A Vehicle class defining speed and color. Object: A real-world instance of a class. Ex: A specific red Ferrari. Encapsulation: Wrapping data and methods into a single unit to protect the data. Ex: A capsule containing medicine; private variables accessed via getters/setters. Abstraction: Hiding complex implementation details and showing only essentials. Ex: Driving a car without knowing how the internal combustion engine works. Inheritance: A child class acquiring properties from a parent class. Ex: Dog inherits from Animal . Polymorphism: One entity taking many forms. Ex: A sound() method that barks for a Dog but meows for a Cat. Write a Java program containing a class, instance variables, constructor, method, and objects class Car { String model; // Instance variable // Constructor Car(String m) { model = m; } // Method void display() { System.out.println("Car Model: " + model); } } public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Car c1 = new Car("Tesla"); // Object creation c1.display(); // Method invocation } } Execution: The JVM enters the main method. It encounters the new keyword, which allocates heap memory for a Car object. The constructor Car("Tesla") is called, initializing the model instance variable to "Tesla".

Finally, the display() method is invoked on the c1 object, printing the output to the console. Java packages and access modifiers Packages group related classes to avoid name clashes. Access Modifiers control the visibility of classes and members. package mypack; public class AccessDemo { private int priv = 1; // Only this class int def = 2; // Only this package protected int prot = 3; // This package + subclasses public int pub = 4; // Everywhere public void show() { System.out.println(priv + def + prot + pub); } } Write a Java program to create a Book class class Book { String title; double price; Book(String t, double p) { title = t; price = p; } void display() { System.out.println("Title: " + title + ", Price: $" + price); } } public class Library { public static void main(String[] args) { Book b1 = new Book("Java Complete Reference", 45.99); Book b2 = new Book("Head First Java", 35.50); b1.display(); b2.display(); } } Classes and Objects in Java in detail A Class is a blueprint. An Object is a physical instance. The new keyword allocates distinct heap memory for every object created. Because each object gets its own memory

block in the heap, they maintain independent copies of instance variables . Changing the variable in one object does not affect the other. class Account { int balance; } public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Account acc1 = new Account(); Account acc2 = new Account(); acc1.balance = 500; acc2.balance = 1000; // acc1 and acc2 are independent. } } Instance variables and local variables in Java Property Instance Variable Local Variable Declaration Inside class, outside methods. Inside a method or block. Memory Stored in the Heap (inside the object). Stored in the Stack . Lifetime Lives as long as the object lives. Destroyed when the method execution completes. Initialization Automatically initialized to defaults (0, null). NO default value. Must be explicitly initialized. Constructors in Java in detail Constructors are special blocks invoked when an object is instantiated via new . Rules: Must have the exact same name as the class. Cannot have a return type. Role: They allocate default or specific values to instance variables the moment the object is born, ensuring the object starts in a valid state. Default Constructor: Generated by the compiler if none exists. Initializes fields to 0/null. No-Argument Constructor: Explicitly written

without parameters to run specific setup code. Parameterized Constructor: Accepts arguments to dynamically set up the object. Constructor overloading and constructor chaining in Java Overloading allows a class to have multiple constructors with different parameters. Chaining allows these constructors to call each other, or call the parent's constructor, to avoid duplicating initialization logic. class Parent { Parent() { System.out.println("Parent init"); } } class Child extends Parent { int x, y; Child() { this(0, 0); // Constructor Chaining via this() } Child(int x, int y) { // Overloaded constructor super(); // Constructor Chaining via super() to Parent this.x = x; this.y = y; } } This keyword in Java The this keyword is a reference to the current executing object. Shadowing: When a parameter has the same name as a field: this.age = age; Method invocation: Explicitly calling another method: this.doWork(); Chaining: Calling another constructor: this(name, age); Passing as Argument: Passing the current instance to an event listener: button.addListener(this); Returning: Used in builder patterns to chain method calls: return this; All four access modifiers in Java — private, default, protected, and public Modifier Same Class Same Package Subclass (Diff Pkg) World (Diff Pkg) private Yes No No No (default) Yes Yes

No No protected Yes Yes Yes No public Yes Yes Yes Yes Example: Use private for sensitive data like passwords. Use public for API methods meant for everyone. Use protected for methods meant to be overridden by subclasses. Character wrapper class in Java Wrapper Classes encapsulate primitive types into objects. The mapping is straight-forward (e.g., int → Integer , char → Character ). Autoboxing is the automatic conversion to wrapper; unboxing is the reverse. Character Class Methods: isLetter('A') → true isDigit('5') → true isWhitespace(' ') → true isUpperCase('A') → true isLowerCase('a') → true String class in Java in detail The String class represents an array of characters. Strings are immutable ; once created, their value cannot change. Literals vs New: String s1 = "Java"; creates/reuses a string in the highly-efficient String Constant Pool . String s2 = new String("Java"); forces a new allocation in the normal Heap. == vs equals(): s1 == s2 compares memory addresses (returns false here). s1.equals(s2) compares the actual text characters (returns true). Methods: length() , substring(start, end) , toUpperCase() , concat(str) . String, StringBuffer, and StringBuilder in Java Feature String StringBuffer StringBuilder Mutability Immutable Mutable Mutable Thread Safety Yes Yes (Synchronized) No (Not Synchronized) Performance

Slow for concat Moderate Fastest StringBuffer Methods: append("A") : Adds "A" to the end. insert(1, "A") : Inserts "A" at index 1. replace(1, 3, "X") : Replaces substring. delete(1, 3) : Removes characters. reverse() : Reverses the sequence.

Unit III: Inheritance & Exceptions Java package A Java package is a mechanism for organizing related classes and interfaces into a single namespace. It prevents naming conflicts and controls access (encapsulation). Two Examples: java.util (Contains utility classes like Scanner, ArrayList) java.lang (Contains core classes like String, Math. It is imported automatically) Inheritance Inheritance is a mechanism where a new class acquires the properties and methods of an existing class, establishing an IS-A relationship and promoting code reuse. Types supported in Java (via classes): Single Inheritance Multilevel Inheritance Hierarchical Inheritance (Note: Multiple and Hybrid inheritance are not supported through classes, only through interfaces). Purpose of the super keyword The super keyword is a reference variable used to refer to the immediate parent class object. Two Uses: To invoke the immediate parent class constructor (e.g., super(); ). To invoke an overridden method in the parent class (e.g., super.display(); ). Object class The Object class (located in the java.lang package) is the root class of the Java class hierarchy. Every class in Java directly or indirectly inherits from the Object class. Two Methods: toString() equals(Object obj) Polymorphism Polymorphism is the ability of an object or method to take on many forms, allowing the

same interface to be used for different underlying forms (data types). Two Types: Compile-time Polymorphism (Static binding, e.g., Method Overloading). Run-time Polymorphism (Dynamic binding, e.g., Method Overriding). Dynamic binding Dynamic Binding is the process where the compiler does not resolve the method call at compile time, but rather the JVM determines the actual method implementation to execute at runtime based on the actual object type. It is called late binding because the binding of the method call to the method body is delayed until the program is actually executing. Upcasting and downcasting in Java Upcasting: Casting a subclass reference variable to a superclass reference. This is done automatically and implicitly by the compiler. Downcasting: Casting a superclass reference variable back to a subclass reference. This must be done explicitly by the programmer and requires checking to prevent ClassCastException . Purpose of the instanceof operator The instanceof operator is a binary operator used to test whether a given object is an instance of a specific class, subclass, or interface. It returns true or false . It is primarily used to check object types before attempting a downcast , preventing runtime exceptions. Abstract class Abstract Class: A class declared with the abstract

keyword that cannot be instantiated. It can contain both abstract methods (without a body) and concrete methods. Interface: A completely "abstract class" that acts as a contract. In modern Java, it primarily contains abstract methods and static constants, though it can now have default methods. A class implements an interface. Generics in Java Generics enable types (classes and interfaces) to be parameters when defining classes, interfaces and methods. This provides stronger type checks at compile time and removes the need for explicit casting. Example: <T> is a generic type parameter where T stands for Type. Example usage: List<String> list = new ArrayList<String>(); Built-in and user-defined packages Built-in Packages: Provided by the Java API. Example: java.util , java.io . User-defined Packages: Created by the programmer to group related classes. Example: package com.mycompany.utils; Import Statement: Used to bring a class or an entire package into visibility so it can be used without typing its fully qualified name (e.g., import java.util.Scanner; ). Single, multilevel, hierarchical, and hybrid inheritance Single: Class B inherits from Class A. (Dog inherits Animal) Multilevel: Class C inherits from Class B, which inherits from Class A. (Puppy inherits Dog inherits Animal) Hierarchical: Multiple classes inherit from a single Class

A. (Dog and Cat both inherit Animal) Hybrid: A combination of two or more types. In Java, true hybrid inheritance involving multiple parents is only achievable via Interfaces to avoid the Diamond Problem. Three major uses of the super keyword Invoke Parent Constructor: super(); (Must be the first line in the child constructor). Invoke Parent Method: Used when the child has overridden the method. super.display(); Access Parent Variable: Used when the child class hides a parent's variable with the same name. System.out.println(super.x); Object class and the purpose of toString(), equals(), hashCode(), and getClass() The Object class is the universal superclass of all Java classes. toString() : Returns a string representation of the object (often overridden to show field values). equals() : Used to compare the logical equality of two objects. hashCode() : Returns an integer hash code value for the object, crucial for collections like HashMap . getClass() : Returns the runtime class object of the current instance (used in reflection). Method overloading and method overriding Method Overloading Method Overriding Occurs within the same class . Occurs between parent and child classes. Parameters must be different. Parameters must be exactly the same. Resolved at Compile-Time (Static Binding). Resolved at Run-Time

(Dynamic Binding). Example: add(int a, int b) vs add(double a, double b) Example: Animal.sound() overridden by Dog.sound() Compile-time and run-time polymorphism in Java Compile-time Polymorphism: Achieved through Method Overloading. The compiler knows exactly which method to call based on the method signature (number and type of arguments). Fast execution because binding happens early. Run-time Polymorphism: Achieved through Method Overriding. A parent reference points to a child object. The JVM determines which overridden method to execute during runtime based on the actual object type , not the reference type. Dynamic binding and object casting Dynamic Binding is resolving a method call at runtime depending on the actual object. Upcasting: Casting a subclass to a superclass. It is automatic. Animal a = new Dog(); This triggers dynamic binding when overridden methods are called. Downcasting: Casting a superclass back to a subclass. It must be explicit. Dog d = (Dog) a; This is needed to access methods specific only to the child class. Instanceof operator and its importance before performing downcasting The instanceof operator checks if an object is an instance of a specific class or interface. Importance in Downcasting: Downcasting a parent reference to a child reference is dangerous because if the

parent reference doesn't actually hold that specific child object, the JVM throws a ClassCastException . Using if (obj instanceof Dog) { Dog d = (Dog) obj; } ensures the downcast is mathematically safe. Abstract class and an interface Abstract Class Interface Can have both abstract and concrete methods. Historically only abstract methods (now allows default methods). Can have state (instance variables). Only public static final constants. A class can extend only one abstract class. A class can implement multiple interfaces. Multiple Inheritance: Java prevents a class from extending multiple classes to avoid ambiguity, but it allows a class to implement multiple interfaces because interfaces (traditionally) have no implementation to clash. Generics and their advantages Generics allow classes, interfaces, and methods to operate on specified data types as parameters, providing compile-time type safety. Advantages: Prevents ClassCastException at runtime and eliminates the need for manual type-casting. Common Parameters: T : Type (General) E : Element (Used heavily in Collections like ArrayList) K : Key (Used in Maps) V : Value (Used in Maps) ArrayList and packages in Java ArrayList: A resizable-array implementation of the List interface found in java.util . Unlike standard arrays, it grows and shrinks dynamically. Common Operations: add() ,

remove() , get() , size() . Packages: Containers that group related classes and interfaces together. Purpose: To prevent naming conflicts, group related code logically, and control access visibility (via package-private modifiers). All major types of inheritance in Java—single, multilevel, hierarchical, hybrid, and multiple inheritance Single: Class A → Class B Multilevel: Class A → Class B → Class C Hierarchical: Class A → Class B, Class A → Class C Multiple: Class A, Class B → Class C. Not supported directly through classes due to the Diamond Problem. Hybrid: A mix of the above. Multiple Inheritance via Interfaces: Because interfaces traditionally do not hold implementation or state, a single Java class can implement multiple interfaces without ambiguity over whose method to inherit. Parent Constructor } void display() { super.show(); // 2. Parent Method System.out.println("Child x: " + x); System.out.println("Parent x: " + super.x); // 3. Parent Variable

Run-time: The JVM binds the sound() method based on whether the actual heap object is an Animal or a Dog . Dynamic binding in detail Dynamic Binding occurs when the compiler cannot determine the method implementation at compile time,

so the JVM resolves it during execution. class Vehicle { void move() { System.out.println("Moving"); } } class Car extends Vehicle { @Override void move() { System.out.println("Driving on wheels"); } } public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Vehicle v = new Car(); // Superclass ref, Subclass object v.move(); // Outputs: Driving on wheels } } At compile time, the compiler ensures move() exists in Vehicle . Unit V: Collections Garbage Collection in Java Garbage Collection (GC) is the process by which Java programs perform automatic memory management, freeing up the heap by deleting objects that are no longer in use. An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when it is completely unreferenced (i.e., no live thread can access it). This happens if its reference is set to null , if it is created anonymously, or if references are reassigned. Garbage Collection and finalization in Java Garbage Collection automatically deallocates memory for objects that are no longer reachable. Eligibility: An object is eligible if its reference is set to null , reassigned, or created anonymously. finalize(): A method in the Object class historically called by the GC just before destroying the object to release non-Java resources. Deprecation: finalize() was deprecated in Java 9 because it is unpredictable, impacts performance, and can cause memory leaks if implemented poorly. Modern Alternatives: Use try-with-resources (implementing AutoCloseable ) for deterministic resource cleanup, or the java.lang.ref.Cleaner API.

title: How many different 4-letter words can be formed using the letters of the word MATH, when each letter can be used only once?
